teile.einleitung: A main group is a vertical column in the periodic table of the elements. All the elements in a main group have the same number of outer electrons and therefore behave similarly in chemistry. In the classic arrangement there are eight main groups.
wichtigste: Main groups are vertical columns in the periodic table.
Classically there are 8 main groups.
Elements of the same main group have the same number of valence electrons.
Main group 3 is called the boron group after its first element; aluminium is also in it.
Main group 4 is called the carbon group; below carbon is silicon.
Main group 6, with oxygen and sulphur, is called the chalcogens.
Many main groups have their own names, such as alkali metals, halogens and noble gases.

abschnitte.text: In the **periodic table**, all the chemical elements are arranged in rows and columns. The rows are called periods, and the vertical columns are called **groups**. The eight groups on the left and right edges are called main groups. Between them are the **transition groups** with metals such as iron, copper and gold. In 1869 the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev was the first to arrange the elements so that similar elements are placed one below another.

Every atom has electrons arranged in shells around the nucleus. The electrons in the outermost shell are called **valence electrons**. They determine how an element reacts with others. For the main groups, the group number equals the number of valence electrons: sodium in main group 1 has one, chlorine in main group 7 has seven. That is why elements in a group react in a similar way, like brothers and sisters with the same characteristics.

Main group 1 is called the **alkali metals**; it includes lithium, sodium and potassium. Main group 2 are the alkaline earth metals such as magnesium and calcium. Group 3 is the **boron group** with boron and aluminium, group 4 the carbon group with carbon, silicon and tin. Group 5 is called the nitrogen group, group 6 the **chalcogens** with oxygen and sulphur. Main group 7 are the halogens such as fluorine and chlorine, group 8 the noble gases such as helium, neon and argon.

Alkali metals are so reactive that they react violently with water. Halogens form salts with metals; table salt, for example, consists of sodium and chlorine. **Noble gases** hardly react at all, because their outer shell is full. That is why light bulbs are filled with argon and neon signs with neon. Within a group, the atoms get larger from top to bottom, and the properties often change step by step too.

Today the international chemistry organisation **IUPAC** recommends numbering all 18 columns in order. The main groups then have the numbers 1, 2 and 13 to 18. So the boron group is group 13, and the noble gases are group 18. In many school books, including in Switzerland, the classic numbering from 1 to 8 is still used, however. Both systems describe the same columns.

begriffe.erklaerung: A table in which all the chemical elements are arranged.
The electrons in the outermost shell of an atom.
Main group 6 with oxygen and sulphur.
Main group 7; the name means “salt formers”.
Main group 8, gases that hardly ever react.

gewusst: Silicon is directly below carbon and is the most important material in computer chips.
Helium is among the noble gases even though it has only two outer electrons.
The name halogens means “salt formers”.

teile.einleitung: Ceramics is a hard material that is shaped from clay and then fired in a kiln. Whether plates, flowerpots, roof tiles or bathroom tiles: we come across ceramics every day. It is one of the oldest materials that people have made themselves.
wichtigste: Ceramics are made mainly from clay.
Only firing in the kiln makes soft clay hard and firm.
Someone who makes crockery from clay is a potter by trade.
Round vessels are shaped on the spinning potter’s wheel.
Porcelain is a particularly fine, white ceramic.
A shiny glaze makes ceramics watertight and beautiful.
Bathroom tiles and red roof tiles are usually made of fired clay.

abschnitte.text: **Ceramics** is a collective term for objects made of fired, non-metallic raw materials. The most important raw material is **clay**, a fine, mouldable earth made of tiny mineral particles. Clay is kneaded with water, shaped and dried. The word ceramics comes from the Greek word “keramos”, which means potter’s clay.

After shaping, the clay must first dry slowly, otherwise it cracks. Then it is fired in a special kiln, depending on the type at about 900 to over 1400 degrees Celsius. At this heat the minerals in the clay change, and the material becomes rock hard. Often a second firing with **glaze** follows, a glassy layer that makes the vessel watertight and shiny. Unfired clay, on the other hand, would go soft again in water.

Roughly speaking, there is **earthenware**, **stoneware** and **porcelain**. Earthenware, such as flowerpots or roof tiles, is porous and is fired at fairly low temperatures. Stoneware is denser and is often used for sturdy crockery. Porcelain is made from kaolin, feldspar and quartz, fired at very high temperatures and is white and sometimes even slightly translucent.

As early as the Stone Age, people shaped figures from clay and fired them in the fire. The oldest known clay vessels come from China and are about 20,000 years old. The **potter’s wheel** was invented about 5000 to 6000 years ago in the Near East. Porcelain was invented in China; in Europe it was only successfully made at the beginning of the 18th century in Meissen.

In the kitchen we use cups, plates and bowls made of ceramics. Houses are built with bricks and roofed with tiles, and floors and walls are covered with tiles. Washbasins and toilet bowls are also made of ceramics, because it is hard, smooth and easy to clean. Modern technical ceramics are found in spark plugs, knife blades, dental crowns and heat shields.

In the Thun and Heimberg region in the canton of Bern, pottery has a long tradition; the colourful Thun majolica is well known. In Langenthal, porcelain was made for many decades. Today there are small pottery studios and courses in many Swiss places, where children can also work at the potter’s wheel.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fine, soft earth that can be kneaded and shaped with water.
Strong heating in a kiln so that the shaped clay becomes hard.
A glassy, shiny layer on ceramics that makes them watertight.
Very fine, white and hard ceramic made from kaolin, feldspar and quartz.
A spinning disc on which round vessels are shaped from clay.

gewusst: Porcelain was once so valuable in Europe that it was called “white gold”.
NASA’s space shuttles were protected from the heat of re-entry by thousands of ceramic tiles.
Because clay shrinks when it dries and is fired, a potter has to make pieces a little larger.

teile.einleitung: Infrared spectroscopy, IR spectroscopy for short, is a method chemists use to find out which building blocks a molecule contains. A substance is irradiated with infrared light and you measure which parts of it the substance absorbs. Because every molecule shows its own pattern, it works almost like a fingerprint.
wichtigste: Infrared radiation mainly makes molecules vibrate.
Each type of bond absorbs infrared light at typical wavenumbers.
A C=O double bond shows a strong band at about 1700 cm⁻¹.
An alcohol O-H group shows a broad band around 3200 to 3550 cm⁻¹.
The region below about 1500 cm⁻¹ is called the fingerprint region.
Wilhelm Herschel discovered infrared radiation in 1800.
The heart of an FTIR spectrometer is a Michelson interferometer.

abschnitte.text: **Infrared radiation** is light that is invisible to our eyes because its waves are longer than those of red light. But we feel it as heat, for example from a radiator or in the sun. It was discovered by the astronomer **Wilhelm Herschel** in 1800. He split sunlight with a prism and put thermometers behind the colours. Next to the red end, where no light could be seen any more, it was warmest.

The atoms in a molecule are joined by bonds that behave like little springs. They can stretch, squash and bend; this is called **molecular vibration**. If infrared light with exactly the right energy hits a molecule, it is absorbed and the vibration becomes stronger. Light atoms vibrate faster than heavy ones, which is why a C-D bond with heavy **deuterium** lies at a lower wavenumber than a C-H bond. Strong bonds also vibrate faster than weak ones.

An **IR spectrum** shows at which wavenumbers a substance absorbs light. The **wavenumber** is given in cm⁻¹ and is the reciprocal of the wavelength, so 2000 cm⁻¹ corresponds to 5 µm. A C=O double bond, for example in acetone, produces a strong band at about 1700 cm⁻¹. Alcohols show a broad O-H band around 3200 to 3550 cm⁻¹ because they form hydrogen bonds. Below about 1500 cm⁻¹ lies the **fingerprint region**, whose pattern is unique for every molecule.

Modern instruments are mostly **FTIR spectrometers**, which stands for Fourier transform infrared. Their heart is a Michelson interferometer with a moving mirror. Instead of measuring each wavenumber separately, the instrument records them all at the same time. A computer then converts the measurement into a spectrum using a mathematical method, the Fourier transform. So a measurement often takes only a few seconds.

Pharmaceutical companies use IR spectroscopy to check whether a medicine contains the right active ingredient. The police use it to examine paint chips, fibres or suspicious powders. In food testing and recycling, it is used to recognise different plastics. Atmospheric scientists also use it, because gases such as **carbon dioxide** and methane absorb infrared radiation and so contribute to the greenhouse effect. Space telescopes such as the James Webb Telescope also observe space in infrared light.

begriffe.erklaerung: Invisible light with long waves that we feel as heat.
The back and forth movement of the atoms in a molecule.
The reciprocal of the wavelength, given in cm⁻¹.
A place in the spectrum where light is absorbed.
Part of the spectrum with a pattern that is unique for every molecule.

gewusst: Herschel actually discovered infrared radiation by chance with completely ordinary thermometers.
Snakes such as pit vipers can sense the infrared radiation of warm prey.
Remote controls send their signals with invisible infrared light.

teile.einleitung: The limewater test is a simple chemical test for detecting the gas carbon dioxide. If you bubble the gas into clear limewater, it turns milky and cloudy. With this experiment you can even show that the air we breathe out contains carbon dioxide.
wichtigste: The limewater test is used to detect carbon dioxide.
Limewater is a solution of calcium hydroxide in water.
Limewater is alkaline.
In a positive test, the limewater turns milky and cloudy.
The cloudiness is caused by finely spread calcium carbonate.
Exhaled air contains about 4 per cent carbon dioxide.
If you keep bubbling carbon dioxide in for a very long time, the solution becomes clear again.

abschnitte.text: **Limewater** is a clear, colourless solution of **calcium hydroxide** in water. Calcium hydroxide is also called slaked lime; it is used, for example, for mortar. Limewater is **alkaline**, that is the opposite of acidic, and can irritate skin and eyes. That is why pupils wear safety goggles when experimenting. It is made by stirring calcium hydroxide into water and filtering off the undissolved remains.

You bubble the gas you want to test into a test tube of limewater. If it contains **carbon dioxide**, this reacts with the calcium hydroxide. Water and **calcium carbonate**, that is chalk, are formed. Calcium carbonate hardly dissolves in water and floats in the liquid as tiny white particles. That is why the limewater turns milky and cloudy, and the test is positive.

A popular school experiment goes like this: you carefully blow breath into limewater through a small tube. After a short time it turns cloudy. This shows that exhaled air contains a lot of carbon dioxide, about **4 per cent**. The air we breathe in, on the other hand, contains only about 0.04 per cent. The body produces carbon dioxide during **cellular respiration**, when it burns nutrients to obtain energy.

If you hold a cold glass over a burning candle and then shake the collected gases with limewater, it turns cloudy. This shows that carbon dioxide is produced when something burns. Because carbon dioxide contains carbon, the **candle wax** must also contain carbon. So with the limewater test you can also find out which elements a substance is made of. The same applies to wood, paper or natural gas.

If you keep bubbling carbon dioxide into the cloudy limewater for a very long time, something surprising happens: the solution becomes clear again. The calcium carbonate turns into **calcium hydrogen carbonate**, which dissolves well in water. Exactly this reaction also takes place in nature when water containing carbonic acid dissolves limestone and forms caves. In a similar way, lime mortar in old walls hardens because it slowly takes up carbon dioxide from the air.

begriffe.erklaerung: A check that shows whether a particular substance is present.
Slaked lime, which dissolved in water gives limewater.
Chalk, which comes out of solution as white cloudiness.
A colourless gas that we breathe out and that is produced when things burn.
The process by which body cells obtain energy and produce carbon dioxide.

gewusst: Exhaled air contains about a hundred times more carbon dioxide than fresh air.
Lime mortar in old walls hardens over many years through the same reaction.
You can neither see nor smell carbon dioxide itself; the limewater makes it visible.

teile.einleitung: In heterogeneous catalysis, a catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction even though it is in a different phase from the substances that react. The catalyst is usually a solid, and the starting substances are gases or liquids. The best-known example is the catalytic converter in a car, which turns poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful substances.
wichtigste: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up itself.
In heterogeneous catalysis, the catalyst and the reaction mixture are in different phases.
The reaction takes place on the surface of the catalyst in three steps: adsorption, reaction, desorption.
A three-way catalytic converter in a car contains mainly platinum, palladium and rhodium.
It breaks down carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides at the same time.
Many important substances such as ammonia, sulphuric acid and nitric acid are made with heterogeneous catalysis.
Gerhard Ertl received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2007 for his studies of reactions on solid surfaces.

abschnitte.text: A **catalyst** is a substance that makes a chemical reaction run faster but itself remains unchanged at the end. It lowers the energy needed for the reaction to start. In **heterogeneous catalysis**, the catalyst and the reacting substances are in different **phases**, for example a solid catalyst and gases. The advantage: the solid catalyst can easily be separated from the products and reused for a long time. That is why this kind of catalysis is particularly important in industry.

The reaction takes place on the **surface** of the catalyst, in three steps. First the particles stick to the surface; this is called **adsorption**. Then they react with each other there, because their bonds have been loosened. Finally the new particles come away again; this is called **desorption**. According to the Sabatier principle, the particles must stick neither too weakly nor too strongly, otherwise the catalyst works badly.

In the exhaust of petrol cars there is a **three-way catalytic converter**. It consists of a ceramic block with many fine channels coated with the precious metals platinum, palladium and rhodium. There, poisonous carbon monoxide, unburnt hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides are turned at the same time into carbon dioxide, water and nitrogen. Cars with a catalytic converter must not be filled with leaded petrol, because lead poisons the active surface. In Switzerland the catalytic converter became practically compulsory for new petrol cars at the end of the 1980s, and leaded petrol is banned today.

Many basic chemicals are made by heterogeneous catalysis. In the **Haber-Bosch process**, ammonia for fertiliser is made from nitrogen and hydrogen on an iron catalyst. In the Ostwald process, ammonia is oxidised on a platinum-rhodium gauze to nitrogen monoxide, which is used to make nitric acid. In the contact process for sulphuric acid, vanadium(V) oxide oxidises sulphur dioxide to sulphur trioxide. And in the **hydrogenation of fats** for margarine, nickel serves as the catalyst.

Catalysis has been honoured several times with the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Wilhelm Ostwald received it in 1909, among other things for his work on catalysis, and Paul Sabatier in 1912. The German chemist **Gerhard Ertl** received the Nobel Prize in 2007 for his studies of chemical processes on solid surfaces. He showed step by step exactly what happens on the surface of a catalyst. Today research is being done on catalysts for producing hydrogen and environmentally friendly fuels.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that speeds up a reaction and is not used up in it.
A region with a uniform state, for example solid, liquid or gas.
Particles sticking to the surface of a solid.
Particles coming away from a surface.
A substance such as lead that blocks the surface of a catalyst.

gewusst: A catalyst must have an enormous surface area, which is why the precious metals are spread out in tiny particles on the support.
A catalytic converter only works properly once it is a few hundred degrees hot, which is why exhaust gases are dirtiest just after starting.
Because platinum, palladium and rhodium are very valuable, old catalytic converters are collected and recycled.

teile.einleitung: A blast furnace is a huge plant in which liquid pig iron is obtained from iron ore. It is as tall as a building of several storeys and works day and night, often for many years without a break. The pig iron is later turned into steel for bridges, cars and rails.
wichtigste: In a blast furnace, iron ore is turned into liquid pig iron with coke.
Coke serves both as fuel and as a reducing agent.
It is mainly the gas carbon monoxide that removes the oxygen from the iron oxide.
Hot air is blown in at the bottom so that the coke burns fiercely.
Limestone binds the waste rock into slag, which floats on top of the pig iron.
Letting the liquid iron run out is called tapping.
Pig iron contains about 4 per cent carbon.

abschnitte.titel: How a blast furnace is built
abschnitte.text: A blast furnace is a tall, round steel shaft lined inside with fireproof bricks. At the top, the **throat**, layers of iron ore, coke and limestone are loaded in turn. At the bottom, nozzles blow in hot air that has first been heated to over 1000 °C in large **hot blast stoves**. Right at the bottom, in the hearth, the liquid iron and the slag collect.

The coke burns with the oxygen of the hot air, and it gets very hot, in places around 2000 °C. This produces the gas **carbon monoxide**, which rises upwards. It takes the oxygen away from the iron oxide in the ore; this process is called **reduction**. What is left is iron, which melts and drips downwards.

Iron ore also contains rock without iron, which is called waste rock. The limestone that is added combines with it to form **slag**. Because the slag is lighter than the iron, it floats on top and can be let out separately. Later it is used as a building material, for example for cement or in road building.

Several times a day a hole is drilled into the bottom of the furnace, and the glowing pig iron flows out. This spectacular moment is called **tapping**. The iron is about 1450 °C hot and glows bright orange. It is then taken to the steelworks in large ladles or wagons.

Because of its high carbon content, pig iron is brittle and cannot be forged. In the steelworks, oxygen is therefore blown into it, which burns off a large part of the carbon. This produces tough, flexible **steel**. There are no blast furnaces in Switzerland any more today; here steel is made mainly from scrap metal in electric furnaces.

As early as the Middle Ages there were simple blast furnaces in Europe that were fired with charcoal. In 1709 the Englishman Abraham Darby used **coke** made from coal for the first time. That was an important step for industrialisation. Iron ore used to be smelted in Switzerland too, for example from the Gonzen mine near Sargans.

begriffe.erklaerung: Iron straight from the blast furnace with a lot of carbon, still brittle.
Almost pure carbon, made by strongly heating coal.
A chemical process in which oxygen is removed from a substance.
Melted rock produced as a by-product of smelting.
Letting the liquid iron run out of the blast furnace.

gewusst: A modern blast furnace can produce several thousand tonnes of pig iron a day.
If a blast furnace is switched off, the iron inside can solidify and destroy the furnace, which is why it runs without a break.

teile.einleitung: Verdigris is a green to bluish green coating that forms when copper comes into contact with vinegar. It is poisonous and must not be eaten or licked. In the past, painters even used verdigris as a bright green paint.
wichtigste: Verdigris forms on copper and metals containing copper, such as brass.
It forms mainly when copper is in contact with vinegar for a long time.
Verdigris is poisonous.
The green layer on old copper roofs is properly called patina.
Patina protects the copper underneath and is therefore not removed.
In the past, painters used verdigris as a green paint.
The German word comes from “Spanish green”.

abschnitte.text: Verdigris is a chemical substance formed from **copper** and **acetic acid**. Chemists call it copper acetate. It forms green to bluish green crusts or powder. Verdigris can form on pure copper and on **brass**, a mixture of copper and zinc. That is why it is sometimes found on old door handles, taps or musical instruments made of brass.

Verdigris is **poisonous**, because copper compounds harm the body in larger amounts. Anyone who swallows it can get stomach ache, nausea and vomiting. So you should not lick greenish spots on copper pans or cutlery. In the past people often cooked in copper pans that were coated with tin inside, so that no verdigris formed in the food. Acidic foods such as pickled gherkins should never be kept in bare copper.

The green layer on old copper roofs, church towers and statues is often called verdigris. Its correct name, however, is **patina**, and it consists mainly of other copper compounds that form with air, rain and carbon dioxide. It usually takes many years for a new copper roof to turn green. Patina is useful, because it protects the copper underneath from further weathering. A famous example is the Statue of Liberty in New York, which is made of copper and is therefore green.

As early as ancient times, people made verdigris on purpose by hanging copper sheets over vinegar. The bright green powder was used as a **pigment** for paintings, book illuminations and murals. Many Renaissance painters also used it. Over time, however, verdigris can turn brown or dark in paintings. Today less poisonous and more durable green pigments are used.

The German word “Grünspan” comes from the medieval expression **“Spanish green”**. It is thought that the pigment was often imported from Spain at that time. In Latin it was called viride hispanicum, which also means Spanish green. In English it is called verdigris, which goes back to the old French “vert de Grèce”, that is “green from Greece”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reddish metal that conducts electricity well and is used for roofs and cables.
A mixture of copper and zinc with a golden yellow colour.
A protective layer that forms on metals over time.
A coloured powder from which paints are made.

gewusst: When it was unveiled, the Statue of Liberty in New York was copper red and only turned green later.
To make verdigris as a paint, people used to hang copper plates over pots of vinegar.
Many church towers in Switzerland have green copper roofs with patina.

teile.einleitung: Jacques Dubochet is a Swiss biophysicist who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2017. He found a way of freezing water so quickly that it becomes solid like glass instead of forming ice crystals. This makes it possible to see tiny building blocks of life in the electron microscope.
wichtigste: Jacques Dubochet was born in Aigle in the canton of Vaud in 1942.
In 2017 he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry together with Joachim Frank and Richard Henderson.
His contribution was to freeze water so quickly that it becomes glassy.
This technique is called vitrification and was developed around 1980 at the EMBL in Heidelberg.
For it, his team plunged thin films of water into liquid ethane.
From 1987 Dubochet was a professor at the University of Lausanne.
His work made cryo-electron microscopy possible.

abschnitte.text: Jacques Dubochet was born in **Aigle** in the canton of Vaud in 1942. As a child he had a reading and spelling difficulty, **dyslexia**, and often found school hard. Even so, he studied physics at what is now the EPFL in Lausanne and then molecular biology in Geneva. Later he did research in Heidelberg and in 1987 became a professor at the **University of Lausanne**. He is known as a researcher with a sense of humour who is committed to society.

An **electron microscope** works with electrons instead of light and can show much smaller things than a normal microscope. So that the electron beam is not disturbed, there is a **vacuum** inside the instrument. Biological samples such as viruses or proteins, however, consist largely of water and dry out in a vacuum. If you freeze them normally, **ice crystals** form. These scatter the electron beam and destroy the fine structures.

Around 1980 Dubochet and his team at the **EMBL** in Heidelberg found a solution. They put the sample in a very thin film of water on a small grid. Then they plunged it in a flash into **liquid ethane**, which had been strongly cooled with liquid nitrogen. The water solidified so quickly that the molecules had no time to form crystals. Glassy ice was formed, and this process is called **vitrification**.

In 2017 Dubochet received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** together with the German-American Joachim Frank and the Briton Richard Henderson. Together they had made **cryo-electron microscopy** possible. Frank developed computing methods to produce a sharp 3D image from many blurry pictures. Henderson showed that this way proteins can be imaged down to individual atoms. This made Dubochet one of the few Swiss Nobel Prize winners in chemistry.

With cryo-electron microscopy, researchers can study the shape of viruses, proteins and other tiny building blocks of life in detail. In 2020, for example, it was used to reveal the structure of the coronavirus very quickly. Such knowledge helps to develop medicines and vaccines. Today there are cryo-electron microscopes in many laboratories all over the world, including at Swiss universities. Dubochet also campaigns for science to be used responsibly for society.

begriffe.erklaerung: A microscope that works with electrons instead of light and shows tiny things.
A space from which almost all the air has been removed.
Freezing water in a flash into glassy ice without crystals.
Electron microscopy of deep-frozen samples.
A difficulty with reading and writing that has nothing to do with intelligence.

gewusst: Dubochet liked to say that he was the first officially recognised dyslexic in the canton of Vaud.
The liquid ethane into which the samples are plunged is colder than minus 150 degrees Celsius.
Glassy ice also occurs in space, for example on comets.

teile.einleitung: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is a formula for calculating the pH of a buffer solution. Buffers are solutions whose pH hardly changes when you add a little acid or alkali. Our blood is also such a buffer.
wichtigste: The equation is: pH equals pKa + lg(c(A⁻) / c(HA)).
It calculates the pH of a buffer solution made of a weak acid and its base.
Karl Albert Hasselbalch formulated the logarithmic form in 1916.
It is derived by taking the logarithm of the expression for the acid dissociation constant.
If acid and base have the same concentration, the pH equals the pKa.
With very dilute buffers or a very uneven ratio it becomes inaccurate.
An acetate buffer with ten times more acetate than acetic acid has a pH of 5.76.

abschnitte.text: A **buffer** is a solution of a weak acid and its matching base, for example acetic acid and acetate. If you add acid, the base mops it up. If you add alkali, the acid mops it up. That is why the **pH** stays almost the same. So buffers work like shock absorbers for the acidity of a solution.

The equation says that pH equals pKa plus the logarithm of the ratio of base to acid. The **pKa** shows how strong an acid is: the smaller it is, the stronger the acid. The base 10 **logarithm** turns a factor of 10 into the number 1. That is why the pH rises by exactly 1 when there is ten times more base than acid. The equation is derived by taking the logarithm of the expression for the acid dissociation constant and rearranging it.

An acetate buffer with a pKa of 4.76 and ten times more acetate than acetic acid has a pH of 4.76 + 1 = 5.76. An ammonia buffer with a pKa of 9.25 and ten times more ammonium than ammonia has a pH of 9.25 minus 1 = 8.25. If you add 0.05 mol of hydrochloric acid to one litre of acetate buffer containing 0.2 mol each of acid and acetate, you get 0.25 mol of acetic acid and 0.15 mol of acetate. The pH then only falls to about 4.54. For a phosphate buffer with a pH of 7.51 and a pKa of 7.21, you need **hydrogen phosphate** and dihydrogen phosphate in a ratio of about 2 to 1.

In 1908 the American chemist and biologist **Lawrence Joseph Henderson** described a formula for the acidity of buffers. In 1916 the Danish doctor **Karl Albert Hasselbalch** rewrote it in the logarithmic form known today. For this he used the pH scale, which the Dane Søren Sørensen had introduced in 1909. Hasselbalch used it above all to study the acidity of blood. That is why the equation is particularly important in medicine and biochemistry.

Human **blood** has a pH of about 7.4 and must stay very precisely at that level. This is ensured mainly by a buffer of carbonic acid and hydrogen carbonate. Doctors use the equation to understand blood values. In laboratories it is used to make buffers for experiments, medicines and measurements. The equation becomes inaccurate with very dilute solutions and when one component is much more common than the other; it usually works well in the range of pKa plus or minus 1.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is.
A solution whose pH hardly changes even when acid or alkali is added.
A measure of the strength of an acid.
A type of calculation that shows how many times you must multiply 10 by itself to get a number.

gewusst: Even a small deviation of the blood pH from 7.4 can become dangerous.
The equation bears the names of two scientists who never worked on it together.
Shampoos and skin creams also contain buffers so that their pH stays stable.

teile.einleitung: The law of conservation of mass is one of the most important basic laws of chemistry. It states that in a chemical reaction no mass is lost and none is newly created. The atoms are only rearranged.
wichtigste: In a chemical reaction, the mass of the products equals the mass of the starting substances.
The atoms do not disappear; they are only joined in new ways.
In a chemical equation, the number of each kind of atom must therefore be the same on both sides.
If matches burn in a sealed jar, the scales show the same mass afterwards.
A candle gets lighter as it burns because mass escapes into the air as gases.
Steel wool gets heavier when it burns because it takes up oxygen from the air.
The law was recognised in the 18th century by Mikhail Lomonosov and Antoine Lavoisier.

abschnitte.text: In every chemical reaction the **total mass** stays the same. The substances present before weigh exactly as much as those present afterwards. The reason: the **atoms** are conserved; they only break old bonds and form new ones. No atom disappears, and none appears out of nowhere. That is why it is called the law of conservation of mass.

A burning candle gets lighter, and yet the law still holds. The wax reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water vapour, and these **gases** escape into the air. With steel wool it is the other way round: it gets heavier when it burns because the iron takes up oxygen from the air. If you carry out such experiments in a **closed system**, for example matches in a sealed jar, the scales show exactly the same mass afterwards.

With the law you can calculate missing masses. If 56 g of iron react completely with 32 g of sulphur, 88 g of iron sulphide are formed. If 12 g of carbon burn with 32 g of oxygen, 44 g of carbon dioxide are formed. If you heat 10 g of limestone and get 5.6 g of quicklime, 4.4 g of gas must have escaped. If a product weighs 50 g and one of the two starting substances 30 g, the other weighed 20 g.

The Russian scholar **Mikhail Lomonosov** described the basic idea as early as the middle of the 18th century. The law became famous mainly through the Frenchman **Antoine Laurent de Lavoisier**, who worked with very precise scales. He carried out combustions in closed vessels and weighed everything before and after. In this way he disproved the phlogiston theory that was widespread at the time, according to which a mysterious substance escapes during burning. Lavoisier is therefore regarded as one of the founders of modern chemistry.

Because atoms are conserved, a correct **chemical equation** must be balanced. To the left and right of the arrow, the number of each kind of atom must be the same. For the formation of water you therefore write 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O: on the left and on the right there are four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms. Balancing such equations is a basic exercise in chemistry lessons.

Strictly speaking, the mass changes by a tiny amount in reactions that release energy. This follows from Albert Einstein’s famous formula E = mc², which shows that energy and mass are linked. In chemical reactions, however, this change is so small that no scales can measure it. In nuclear reactions in nuclear power stations or in the Sun, on the other hand, the effect is clear.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much an object or substance weighs, measured for example in grams.
An experiment in which no substance can get in or out.
A way of writing that shows which substances react and which are formed.
A substance that people used to wrongly believe was in all burnable things.

gewusst: For his experiments Lavoisier had scales built that were among the most precise of his time.
A tree consists largely of carbon, which it has taken in from the air as carbon dioxide.
A nail also gets heavier when it rusts because it takes up oxygen and water from its surroundings.

teile.einleitung: The glowing splint test is a simple experiment that shows whether oxygen is present. A glowing wooden splint is held in a container: if it bursts into a bright flame, there is a lot of oxygen inside. It is one of the best-known experiments in chemistry lessons.
wichtigste: A glowing splint is a wooden splint that glows but does not burn with a flame.
In a positive glowing splint test, the glowing splint bursts into a bright flame.
In normal air the splint does not relight, because air contains only about 21 per cent oxygen.
In carbon dioxide a glowing splint goes out.
Oxygen is oxidising and carries the hazard symbol of a flame over a circle.
The valves of oxygen cylinders must never be oiled or greased.
Water plants produce oxygen through photosynthesis, which can be detected with the glowing splint.

abschnitte.text: You light a thin wooden splint and blow out the flame after a short time. The tip now goes on glowing red; it **smoulders**. You hold this glowing splint in a test tube in which you suspect there is oxygen. If the splint bursts into a bright flame, the test is **positive**: the tube contains pure oxygen or air with a lot of oxygen.

Burning needs fuel, heat and oxygen. Normal air consists of only about 21 per cent oxygen and about 78 per cent nitrogen, which does not burn. In pure oxygen, many more oxygen particles hit the hot wood, and burning is much more vigorous. That is why the glow suddenly turns back into a bright flame. In carbon dioxide, on the other hand, the splint goes out because there is no oxygen.

A classic school experiment shows that plants produce oxygen. You place a water plant such as **Canadian waterweed** under an upturned funnel filled with water and put it in the light. During **photosynthesis**, small gas bubbles rise and collect in a test tube. If you then hold a glowing splint in it, it bursts into flame. In the laboratory you can also obtain oxygen from hydrogen peroxide by adding a little manganese dioxide.

There are separate tests for other gases. **Hydrogen** is detected with the squeaky pop test: a test tube containing the gas is held to a flame, and there is a whistling or barking sound. Carbon dioxide turns clear limewater cloudy. So the glowing splint test is just one of several simple methods for telling gases apart.

Pure oxygen does not burn itself, but it is **oxidising**: it makes other substances burn much more fiercely. Cylinders of pure oxygen therefore carry the hazard symbol with a flame over a circle. Oil and grease can ignite violently in pure oxygen, so the valves of oxygen cylinders must never be lubricated. You always wear safety goggles during experiments.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wooden splint that glows but does not burn with an open flame.
Strongly helps other substances to burn without burning itself.
An experiment that shows that a particular substance is present.
The process in which plants use light to make sugar and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water.

gewusst: Oxygen was discovered independently by Carl Wilhelm Scheele and Joseph Priestley in the 1770s.
In hospitals, patients are given pure oxygen, which is why open fire is strictly forbidden there.
A piece of steel wool that only glows in air burns with bright sparks in pure oxygen.

teile.einleitung: The freezing point is the temperature at which a liquid becomes solid. For water it is 0 degrees Celsius: if it gets colder, a puddle turns into ice. Every substance has its own freezing point.
wichtigste: Water freezes into ice at 0 degrees Celsius.
At minus 5 degrees a puddle freezes, because minus means colder than 0 degrees.
Weather with temperatures below 0 degrees is called frost.
In the freezer, food is kept at about minus 18 degrees.
Salt and antifreeze lower the freezing point of water.
Freezing rain on cold ground forms dangerous black ice.
Frozen water expands, which is why ice floats.

abschnitte.text: When a liquid is cooled, its particles move more and more slowly. At the **freezing point** they settle into a fixed arrangement, and the liquid becomes a solid. For pure water this happens at 0 degrees Celsius. The other way round, ice melts again at exactly this temperature, so the freezing point is the same as the **melting point**. On a thermometer, “minus 10 degrees” means that it is 10 degrees colder than the freezing point of water.

In 1742 the Swedish scientist **Anders Celsius** proposed a temperature scale based on water. Today the rule is: 0 degrees is the freezing point and 100 degrees the boiling point of water at normal air pressure. Celsius himself originally set the scale the other way round, with 100 for the freezing point. In the USA people still use the Fahrenheit scale, where water freezes at 32 degrees Fahrenheit.

Most substances shrink when they solidify, but water expands, by about a tenth. That is why **ice** floats on water and lakes freeze from the top down. Fish survive the winter in the cool water underneath. However, the expansion can also burst water pipes and glass bottles and split rocks in the mountains.

If you dissolve salt or other substances in water, it only freezes at lower temperatures. This effect is called **freezing point depression**. That is why gritting crews spread salt on roads against black ice, and why antifreeze is added to the windscreen washer water in cars. Seawater only freezes at about minus 2 degrees. Other substances have completely different freezing points: mercury solidifies at about minus 39 degrees, and olive oil already turns cloudy and thick in the fridge.

Below 0 degrees we speak of **frost**. If rain freezes instantly on the cold ground, mirror-smooth **black ice** forms. In thunderclouds, water droplets freeze into hailstones, which are sometimes as big as walnuts. You should never touch an ice-cold metal pole with your tongue, because the moist tongue can freeze to it immediately. Then lukewarm water helps; do not pull!

In cold winters some lakes in Switzerland freeze over, for example the Lac de Joux in the Jura or mountain lakes in the Engadine. On frozen Lake St Moritz there are even horse races in February, the **White Turf**. Before you walk onto a lake, however, the ice must have been checked and declared safe by experts. Ice can be thin even where you do not expect it.

begriffe.erklaerung: Temperature at which a liquid becomes solid; for water 0 degrees Celsius.
Temperature at which a solid becomes liquid.
Temperatures below 0 degrees Celsius.
A smooth layer of ice that forms when rain freezes on cold ground.
The lowering of the freezing point when substances such as salt are dissolved in water.

gewusst: Very clean water can be cooled below 0 degrees without freezing, until a small jolt suddenly turns it into ice.
A full glass bottle in the freezer can burst because the freezing water expands.
Hoar frost on branches forms when water vapour in the air turns directly into fine ice crystals during frost.

teile.einleitung: Wood ash is the grey powder left behind when wood has burnt in a fireplace, stove or campfire. It consists of the minerals that cannot burn. Because embers can stay hidden in it for a long time, it must be handled carefully.
wichtigste: Wood ash is usually grey.
Ash is much lighter than the wood was before.
The still glowing remains of a fire are called embers.
There can still be embers in fresh ash, so you do not tip it straight into a rubbish bag.
The safest way to keep fresh ash is in a metal bucket with a lid.
Ash that has cooled down completely goes in the rubbish bag.
In the past, people made soap from wood ash and fat.
Some gardeners use wood ash as fertiliser.

abschnitte.text: Wood consists mainly of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. When it burns, these substances turn into gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour and rise into the air. All that is left are the **minerals** that the tree took up from the soil. That is why the ash is much lighter than the wood, usually less than a hundredth of its weight. It contains mainly calcium, **potassium** and magnesium.

**Embers** can stay hidden in ash for a very long time, sometimes even several days. From the outside, the ash then looks quite harmless and grey. If you tip it into a plastic bag or a cardboard box too early, a fire can start. That is why fresh ash is put in a **metal bucket with a lid** and placed outside on ground that cannot burn. Only when the ash has cooled down completely does it go in the rubbish bag.

Wood ash is **alkaline**, that is the opposite of acidic. If you pour water over it, you get an alkaline solution that used to be called lye. People used it to wash clothes before there was washing powder. If you boil the lye with fat, you get **soap**. The potassium carbonate from the ash used to be called **potash**, because it was boiled down in pots.

Because ash contains potassium and calcium, some gardeners use it as **fertiliser** or sprinkle it against slugs. However, you should only use a little of it, because ash makes the soil less acidic and can also harm it. Wood ash can also contain heavy metals that the tree took up from the soil. Swiss specialist agencies therefore recommend always disposing of ash with the household rubbish. Ash from painted, varnished or treated wood never belongs in the garden.

Potash from wood ash used to be an important raw material for making **glass**. Glassmakers needed huge amounts of wood for it; whole forests were cut down. Ash was also used for dyeing fabrics and tanning leather. People also talk about ash from volcanoes, but this consists of finely ground rock and has nothing to do with burnt wood.

begriffe.erklaerung: The still glowing remains of a fire.
Substances such as potassium and calcium that plants take up from the soil.
The opposite of acidic; also called basic.
A salt from wood ash; chemically potassium carbonate.

gewusst: From a cubic metre of stacked wood, only a small bucket of ash is left.
In a heap of ash, embers can go on smouldering days after the fire.
The chemical element potassium takes its name from potash.

teile.einleitung: The rate constant k is a number that shows how fast a chemical reaction takes place. It appears in the rate law and links the reaction rate to the concentrations of the starting substances. The larger k, the faster the reaction.
wichtigste: The rate law for A + B → products is generally v = k·c(A)^m·c(B)^n.
The rate constant k does not depend on the concentration of the reactants.
However, k depends strongly on temperature and on catalysts.
For a first-order reaction k has the unit s⁻¹, for a second-order reaction L/(mol·s).
For first-order reactions the half-life is t½ = ln 2 / k.
The equilibrium constant is the ratio K = k(forward) / k(reverse).

abschnitte.text: The **reaction rate** v shows how fast the concentration of a substance changes during a reaction, for example in moles per litre and second. It usually depends on the concentrations of the starting substances, the **reactants**. The rate law describes this relationship: v = k·c(A)^m·c(B)^n. The number k is the **rate constant**; it is characteristic of each reaction at a particular temperature. The exponents m and n have to be determined by experiment.

The sum of the exponents is called the **reaction order**. For a first-order reaction v = k·c, and k has the unit s⁻¹. An example: with k = 0.05 s⁻¹ and c = 0.2 mol/L you get v = 0.01 mol/(L·s). For a second-order reaction such as v = k·c(A)·c(B), k has the unit L/(mol·s). With k = 2 L/(mol·s) and both concentrations 0.1 mol/L you get v = 0.02 mol/(L·s).

The **half-life** is the time after which only half of a substance is left. For first-order reactions it does not depend on the starting concentration and is t½ = ln 2 / k, or about 0.693 / k. With k = 0.0231 per minute this gives exactly 30 minutes. Radioactive substances decay according to the same law, and many medicines are also broken down in the body in roughly this way.

Concentration does not change k, but temperature certainly does. A rule of thumb is the **RGT rule** (reaction rate and temperature rule): if the temperature rises by 10 degrees, a reaction becomes about two to four times faster. This is described more precisely by the Arrhenius equation, named after the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius, who put it forward in 1889. A **catalyst** increases k because it offers the reaction an easier route with lower activation energy. That is why food keeps longer in a cool fridge: the reactions that make it go off run more slowly.

Many reactions run in both directions, forwards and backwards. In **chemical equilibrium** both rates are equal, and the concentrations no longer change. It follows that the equilibrium constant K equals the ratio of the two rate constants: K = k(forward) / k(reverse). If the forward reaction is much faster than the reverse reaction, the equilibrium lies far on the side of the products.

begriffe.erklaerung: How fast the concentration of a substance changes during a reaction.
Starting substance of a chemical reaction.
Sum of the exponents in the rate law.
Time after which only half of a substance is still present.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.

gewusst: The rate constants of different reactions can differ by many powers of ten, from fractions of a second to thousands of years.
The catalytic converter in a car speeds up reactions that turn poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful substances.
Svante Arrhenius received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1903.

teile.einleitung: The Grätzel cell is a special solar cell that uses a dye to turn sunlight into electricity. It was invented by the chemist Michael Grätzel at the EPFL in Lausanne. Its model is the photosynthesis of plants.
wichtigste: The Grätzel cell is also called a dye-sensitised solar cell.
Michael Grätzel developed it at the EPFL in Lausanne.
Its model was photosynthesis, in which leaf green captures light.
A dye captures the light and passes electrons to titanium dioxide.
The classic electrolyte contains iodide and triiodide.
Ruthenium complexes were the classic dyes used.
The cell also works well in diffuse light.
Michael Grätzel received the Millennium Technology Prize for it in 2010.

abschnitte.text: The Grätzel cell is a **dye-sensitised solar cell**. It turns light into electricity, much like the familiar blue solar cells on house roofs. Instead of silicon, however, it uses a dye that captures the light. The cells can be transparent and coloured, for example red, orange or green. This means they can easily be built into windows and façades.

Plants capture sunlight with the green pigment **chlorophyll** and use the energy in **photosynthesis**. Michael Grätzel transferred this idea to technology. In his cell, an artificial dye takes over the job of leaf green. That is why people sometimes speak of “artificial photosynthesis”. However, the cell does not make sugar but electricity.

Between two glass plates there is a layer of tiny grains of **titanium dioxide**, a white substance that is also found in toothpaste and paint. The dye sticks to the grains, classically a **ruthenium complex**. When light hits the dye, it passes an electron to the titanium dioxide, and this flows through a wire as electricity. A liquid, the **electrolyte** with iodide and triiodide, then gives the dye an electron back. In this way the cycle keeps going as long as light shines.

Michael Grätzel is a chemist who was born in Germany in 1944 and has done research at the **EPFL** in Lausanne for decades. In 1991 he presented the cell together with Brian O'Regan in the scientific journal Nature. For the invention he received the **Millennium Technology Prize** in Finland in 2010, one of the most important technology prizes in the world. On the EPFL campus, the SwissTech Convention Center has a coloured glass façade with dye-sensitised solar cells.

A big advantage is that the cell also works well in **diffuse light**, that is when it is cloudy or indoors. It is light, can be coloured and transparent and needs relatively simple materials. On the other hand, its efficiency is usually lower than that of good silicon cells. In addition, the liquid inside can leak or change over time. Today small Grätzel cells supply electricity, for example, to sensors or computer keyboards indoors.

begriffe.erklaerung: A component that turns light directly into electricity.
The process by which plants make sugar from light, water and carbon dioxide.
A white substance that takes up the electrons in the cell and passes them on.
A liquid in which electrically charged particles can move.
How much of the light energy shining in is actually turned into electricity.

gewusst: In school lessons you can even build simple dye-sensitised solar cells with raspberry or blackberry juice.
The façade of the SwissTech Convention Center in Lausanne produces electricity with colourful glass panes.
Grätzel cells can produce electricity from the light of a room lamp.

teile.einleitung: Limestone and acid react vigorously with each other: if you drip acid onto limestone, it fizzes and gas bubbles form. The limestone dissolves and carbon dioxide is produced. Geologists use this reaction in the field and we all use it when descaling at home, and it even shapes whole caves.
wichtigste: Limestone consists mainly of calcium carbonate with the formula CaCO3.
When an acid reacts with limestone, it fizzes and gas bubbles form.
Hydrochloric acid and calcium carbonate give calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide.
Geologists use dilute hydrochloric acid to test whether a rock contains limestone.
A raw eggshell dissolves in vinegar within a day.
Limestone caves form when water containing carbonic acid slowly dissolves limestone.
The Jura consists largely of limestone.
Chalk also consists mainly of calcium carbonate.

abschnitte.text: By **limestone** we usually mean calcium carbonate, chemically **CaCO3**. It consists of calcium, carbon and oxygen. Limestone, marble and **chalk** are made mainly of it, and so are mussel shells, corals and eggshells. Many limestones formed from the shells of tiny sea creatures that were deposited on the sea floor millions of years ago. The white coating in the kettle is also calcium carbonate from tap water.

If you put an acid on limestone, **carbon dioxide** is produced and fizzes up as gas bubbles. With hydrochloric acid the reaction is: calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid give calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide. Calcium chloride dissolves in water, which is why the limestone disappears. If you put a raw egg in vinegar for a day, the shell dissolves, and what is left is an egg with a soft skin. The stronger and more concentrated the acid, the more vigorously it fizzes.

In the field, geologists often carry a small bottle of **dilute hydrochloric acid**. They drip a little of it onto a rock. If it fizzes, the rock contains limestone. Granite or gneiss from the Alps, on the other hand, do not fizz. This way rocks can be told apart quickly without needing a laboratory.

Rainwater takes up carbon dioxide from the air and soil and so becomes weak **carbonic acid**. When it seeps through limestone, it slowly dissolves it over thousands of years. This creates cracks, sinkholes and large caves; such a landscape is called **karst**. The **Jura** and many mountains of the Prealps, such as the Säntis or Pilatus, are made of limestone. In the Muotatal in the canton of Schwyz lies the Hölloch, one of the longest cave systems in the world.

abschnitte.titel: Limestone and acid in everyday life
abschnitte.text: Kettles, coffee machines and shower heads are descaled with vinegar or **citric acid**. Over time, acid rain can damage statues and buildings made of limestone or marble. In the sea, extra carbon dioxide makes the water a little more acidic, which makes it harder for corals and mussels to build their shells. Acids from food and drinks also attack tooth enamel, which is why brushing your teeth is important. In building, lime is an important raw material for cement and mortar.

begriffe.erklaerung: The chemical substance that limestone, chalk and marble are made of.
A substance that tastes sour and can dissolve limestone, for example vinegar.
A colourless gas produced when limestone reacts with acid.
A landscape with caves and sinkholes formed by dissolved limestone.

gewusst: More than 200 kilometres of the Hölloch in the Muotatal have been explored.
You can carefully bounce an egg without a shell from the vinegar experiment.
The White Cliffs of Dover in England consist of chalk, that is the shells of tiny sea creatures.

teile.einleitung: The GHS hazard pictograms are nine warning signs for dangerous chemicals that are the same all over the world. They show a black symbol in a white diamond with a red border. Together with signal words and hazard statements, they say exactly what danger a substance poses.
wichtigste: GHS stands for “Globally Harmonised System” for classifying and labelling chemicals.
There are nine different GHS hazard pictograms.
The labels carry the signal words “Danger” or “Warning”.
The standardised hazard statements are called H statements.
A drain cleaner often carries the pictogram for corrosive substances.
An exclamation mark means irritant or harmful to health.
Before, Switzerland used black symbols on orange squares.

abschnitte.text: **GHS** is the abbreviation for the Globally Harmonised System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals. It was drawn up by the United Nations and published in the early 2000s. The aim is for dangerous substances to be labelled in the same way all over the world. Switzerland and the EU have adopted the system and replaced the old orange symbols.

There are nine **pictograms**: exploding bomb, flame, flame over circle, gas cylinder, corrosion, skull and crossbones, exclamation mark, health hazard and environment. The gas cylinder stands for gases under pressure. The upper body of a person with a star on the chest warns of serious damage to health, such as cancer or lung damage. The exclamation mark stands for irritant or harmful substances.

Besides the pictograms, a GHS label contains a **signal word**. “Danger” is used for serious hazards, “Warning” for less serious ones. In addition there are the **H statements**, standardised hazard statements such as “Causes serious eye damage”. The **P statements** give safety advice, for example “Keep out of reach of children”.

A drain cleaner often carries the pictogram for **corrosive** substances, because it can injure skin and eyes. Methylated spirits and barbecue lighter fluid show the flame. Some spray cans carry the flame and the gas cylinder at the same time, because they contain a flammable gas under pressure. Plant protection products often show the environment pictogram with a tree and a fish.

Before you use a product with a GHS pictogram, read the label carefully. Often you need gloves or safety goggles, and you should air the room well. You must never mix different cleaning products, because poisonous gases can form. In case of an accident, Tox Info Suisse can help on the telephone number 145.

begriffe.erklaerung: A simple picture symbol that communicates something without words.
A word on the label that shows how great the danger is: “Danger” or “Warning”.
Standardised sentences that describe the hazard of a substance.
Standardised sentences with advice on how to protect yourself.

gewusst: Each GHS pictogram has a number from GHS01 for the bomb to GHS09 for the environment.
For transport by road and rail there are separate hazard labels that look different from the GHS pictograms.
If you mix a cleaning product containing chlorine with an acidic descaler, poisonous chlorine gas can form.

teile.einleitung: Helium is a colourless, odourless gas that makes party balloons float upwards. It is the second lightest element after hydrogen and belongs to the noble gases. It was named after the Sun, because that is where it was first discovered.
wichtigste: Helium has the atomic number 2 and is the second lightest gas after hydrogen.
It is colourless, odourless and tasteless.
Helium does not burn and reacts with practically no other substance.
The name comes from the Greek word “helios” for Sun.
Helium balloons shrink after a few days because the gas escapes through the skin.
Modern airships are filled with helium.
Breathing in helium from balloons is dangerous because you then get too little oxygen.

abschnitte.text: In 1868, during a solar eclipse, scientists observed a yellow line in the light of the Sun that did not match any known element. The Englishman Norman Lockyer suspected a new element and named it **helium** after the Sun. Only in 1895 did the chemist William Ramsay find helium on Earth too, in a mineral. In space, helium is the second most common element of all after hydrogen.

Helium is about seven times lighter than air. That is why it creates a strong **buoyancy** and makes balloons rise. In the past, airships were filled with hydrogen, but it burns very easily. Because helium is not flammable, today’s airships and weather balloons are much safer with it.

Helium belongs to the **noble gases**, which form almost no chemical compounds. Its atoms are so small that they slip through thin rubber skins. That is why a latex balloon sinks to the ground after one or two days, while foil balloons last longer. Helium only becomes liquid at about minus 269 °C; no other substance has to get this cold before it turns liquid.

Liquid helium cools the powerful magnets in hospitals that are used to make an **MRI** scan of the inside of the body. Divers breathe gas mixtures containing helium on very deep dives. In research too, for example at the CERN particle accelerator in Geneva, helium cools huge magnets. It also protects the hot metal from the air during welding.

If you breathe in helium, you suddenly speak with a high, funny voice. This is because sound travels about three times faster in helium than in air. Even so, it is dangerous, because there is then no **oxygen** in your lungs. You can faint, so you should never try it.

On Earth, helium forms very slowly when radioactive rocks decay. It collects underground together with **natural gas** and is extracted from it. Whatever escapes into the air rises all the way into space and is lost. That is why experts warn against wasting this valuable gas.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas that hardly ever reacts with other substances, for example helium or neon.
A force that pushes a light object upwards in heavier surroundings.
The number of an element in the periodic table; it gives the number of protons.
A coloured line in split light by which an element can be recognised.

gewusst: Helium was discovered on the Sun almost 30 years before it was found on Earth.
At normal air pressure, helium does not become solid even at absolute zero.
The balloon Breitling Orbiter 3, in which Bertrand Piccard flew round the Earth in 1999, was partly filled with helium.

teile.einleitung: Gold is a rare, shiny yellow precious metal that has fascinated people for thousands of years. It does not rust, is very heavy and can be beaten wafer-thin. To this day gold is used for jewellery, as an investment and in technology.
wichtigste: Gold is a chemical element with the symbol Au and the atomic number 79.
Pure gold shines yellow and does not rust.
Gold is very heavy: a cube with sides of 10 cm weighs over 19 kilograms.
Gold can be beaten into wafer-thin gold leaf.
A rectangular block of pure gold is called a gold bar.
The Swiss National Bank keeps Switzerland’s gold.
In the Napf area people still pan gold from the streams today.
The Vreneli is the best-known old Swiss gold coin.

abschnitte.text: Gold is a **precious metal**, which means it hardly reacts with air, water or acids. That is why it does not rust and still shines like new even after thousands of years. Its **density** is about 19.3 grams per cubic centimetre, almost twice that of lead. Gold melts at around 1064 degrees Celsius. It is very soft and stretchy; it can be drawn into fine wires or beaten into foils.

Coins were already being minted from gold over 2500 years ago. In Switzerland the **Vreneli** is famous, a 20-franc gold coin with the head of Helvetia, which was minted from 1897. Today gold coins are no longer used for everyday payments, but they are popular collector’s items and investments. The **Swiss National Bank** owns about 1040 tonnes of gold. A large part of it is stored in Switzerland, the rest in Great Britain and Canada.

Gold is found in veins of rock deep underground or as small grains in the sand of rivers. Large amounts are mined today in China, Australia, Russia and other countries. In Switzerland, hobby gold prospectors pan gold from the streams in the **Napf area** between Lucerne and Bern. For this they use a flat **gold pan**, in which the heavy gold stays behind while lighter sand is washed away. The flakes are usually tiny; you will not get rich this way.

Most pieces of gold jewellery are not made of pure gold but of an **alloy**, that is a mixture with silver or copper. This makes the jewellery harder. Purity is given in **carats**: 24 carats means pure gold. **Gold leaf** is so thin that light shines through it; it is used to gild picture frames, church domes and even cakes. The ancient Egyptians already made magnificent gold masks, for example for the pharaoh Tutankhamun.

Because gold conducts electricity very well and never rusts, it is found in almost every mobile phone and computer. There it coats tiny contacts and connectors. Gold is also used in space travel, for example as a thin layer on the visors of astronauts’ helmets to keep out solar radiation. Dentists used to use gold often for crowns and fillings. Old gold from electronic waste can be recycled.

begriffe.erklaerung: A metal that hardly reacts with air and water and therefore does not rust.
A measure of the purity of gold; 24 carats is pure gold.
A mixture of two or more metals.
Gold that has been beaten into wafer-thin sheets.
A rectangular block of pure gold.

gewusst: All the gold ever mined would fit into a cube with sides of only about 22 metres.
Gold leaf can be thinner than a ten-thousandth of a millimetre.
Gold from ancient graves still shines today just as it did thousands of years ago.

teile.einleitung: The halogens are a family of chemical elements that includes fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine. Their name comes from Greek and means “salt formers”, because with metals they form salts such as our table salt. Halogens are very reactive and are therefore almost never found in nature as pure substances.
wichtigste: The halogens are in main group 7 of the periodic table.
The group includes fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, radioactive astatine and the artificially made tennessine.
Fluorine is the most reactive halogen; reactivity decreases going down the group.
At room temperature fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is liquid and iodine is solid.
Halogens occur as molecules of two atoms, for example Cl₂.
If you dissolve hydrogen chloride in water, you get hydrochloric acid.
In the swimming pool, chlorine kills germs.

abschnitte.titel: A family in the periodic table
abschnitte.text: The halogens form main group 7, which today is also called group 17. All halogen atoms have seven electrons in their outermost shell. So they are missing only a single electron to reach the stable **noble gas configuration**. That is why they readily grab an electron from other atoms and become negatively charged **halide ions**.

Fluorine is a pale yellow gas, chlorine a yellowish green gas with a sharp smell. **Bromine** is a dark reddish brown liquid that gives off poisonous fumes even at room temperature. **Iodine** forms shiny greyish black crystals that turn directly into a violet vapour when warmed. Astatine is radioactive and so rare that only tiny amounts of it exist on the whole Earth.

When a halogen reacts with a metal, a salt is formed. The best-known example is **sodium chloride**, that is our table salt made of sodium and chlorine. Large amounts of chloride, bromide and iodide are also dissolved in seawater. Hydrogen chloride dissolved in water gives **hydrochloric acid**, which by the way is also found in our stomach.

In the swimming pool, **chlorine** makes sure that bacteria and other germs are killed. Fluoride in toothpaste hardens tooth enamel and protects against tooth decay. Our body needs iodine for the thyroid gland, which is why iodine is added to table salt in Switzerland. Chlorine is also used to make plastics such as PVC.

Pure halogens are poisonous and attack skin, eyes and airways. **Fluorine** in particular is so aggressive that it can even attack glass. Chlorine gas is heavier than air and therefore collects near the ground. You must also never mix chlorine cleaners with other cleaning products, because poisonous gases can form.

In 1774 the Swede Carl Wilhelm Scheele was the first to make chlorine. Iodine was discovered in 1811 in the ash of seaweed, bromine in 1826 in salt water. Fluorine could only be produced in pure form in 1886, by the Frenchman **Henri Moissan**, who later received the Nobel Prize for it. Before that, many chemists had been injured in experiments with fluorine.

begriffe.erklaerung: A chemical element from main group 7 that forms salts with metals.
A negatively charged ion of a halogen, for example chloride.
A solution of hydrogen chloride in water, a strong acid.
Changing directly from solid to gas without becoming liquid.

gewusst: Switzerland was one of the first countries in the world to introduce iodised table salt to prevent goitre.
Apart from mercury, bromine is the only element that is liquid at room temperature.
Fluorine is so reactive that it even reacts with some noble gases.

teile.einleitung: A candle is a piece of wax with a wick in the middle that gives light and warmth when it burns. In the past it was one of the most important sources of light; today it is mainly used to create atmosphere. An amazing number of chemical processes take place in the small flame.
wichtigste: A candle is usually made of wax.
The wick is usually made of cotton.
Close to the flame, the wax becomes liquid.
In fact it is not the liquid wax that burns, but its vapour.
Bees supply wax for candles.
A candle is put on a firm candle holder and never next to a curtain.
Before leaving the room, you put out the candle.

abschnitte.text: A candle consists of a fuel, usually **wax**, and a **wick** of braided cotton. Today most candles are made of **paraffin wax**, which is obtained from crude oil. Others are made of stearin, which comes from plant or animal fats. Candles made of beeswax smell particularly nice.

The flame melts the wax right around the wick, so a small pool of liquid wax forms. The liquid wax rises up the wick, much like water in a paper towel; this is called **capillary action**. At the top, the heat turns the wax into **wax vapour**. This vapour combines with the oxygen in the air and burns, producing light, heat, carbon dioxide and water vapour.

abschnitte.titel: A close look at the flame
abschnitte.text: A candle flame has different zones. At the bottom by the wick it is bluish; there the gas burns with plenty of oxygen. The bright yellow part glows because tiny **soot particles** are glowing. The flame is hottest in the outer edge, where you can hardly see it.

The Romans already made candles from beeswax and from **tallow**, that is animal fat. Tallow candles smelt unpleasant and were sooty; beeswax was expensive and mainly for churches and rich people. In the 19th century stearin and paraffin candles came along, which were cheaper. The English scientist Michael Faraday gave famous lectures for children about the candle.

Candles burn on birthday cakes, on the Advent wreath and on the Christmas tree. In many religions, candles are lit during services and in remembrance. In Switzerland, **candle dipping** is popular during Advent: you dip a wick into liquid wax again and again. With every layer the candle gets a little thicker.

A candle is always placed on a firm **candle holder** that cannot burn. Curtains, paper and fir branches must be far enough away, because they can catch fire. Before you leave the room or go to sleep, you put out every candle. Children only light candles together with adults.

begriffe.erklaerung: The thread in the middle of the candle on which the flame burns.
A wax made from crude oil.
Liquid rising by itself in fine fibres or tubes.
Solid animal fat from which candles used to be made.

gewusst: If you blow out a candle and immediately hold a match to the smoke, the flame jumps back onto the wick.
A candle flame in weightlessness is not pointed but round and bluish.
In the past, people also measured time with marked candles, called candle clocks.

teile.einleitung: Wood is the solid material that the trunks, branches and roots of trees and shrubs are made of. It is one of humanity’s oldest materials and grows back again and again. We build houses and furniture with it, use it for heating and even make paper from it.
wichtigste: Wood is obtained from trees.
It consists mainly of cellulose and lignin.
You can read the age of a tree from the annual rings in its trunk.
Dry wood usually floats in water.
Wood conducts heat poorly, which is why a wooden spoon in a pan does not get hot.
The spruce is the most common tree in Swiss forests.
Wood that stays wet for a long time rots.

abschnitte.text: Wood is built up from countless tiny **cells** that look like long little tubes. Their walls consist mainly of **cellulose**, which gives wood its tensile strength. **Lignin** glues the cells together and makes the wood hard and able to withstand pressure. Air is trapped in the hollow spaces, which is why wood is light and usually floats.

In spring a tree grows quickly and forms light, loose wood. In summer the wood becomes darker and denser. In this way a new **annual ring** forms every year, which you can see in a cross-section of the trunk. If you count the rings, you know the age of the tree, and wide rings show good growing years.

When wood burns, it reacts with the oxygen in the air, producing heat, light, water vapour and **carbon dioxide**. A little ash with minerals is left behind. While growing, the tree took in exactly as much carbon dioxide from the air. That is why wood is regarded as a renewable fuel that harms the climate less than oil.

Wood can be sawn, planed, carved and bent. The **joiner** makes furniture and windows from it, the carpenter whole roof structures and wooden houses. Wood conducts heat and electricity poorly and therefore insulates well. Damp wood, however, is attacked by fungi and rots if it is not protected.

About a third of Switzerland is covered with forest. The most common tree is the **spruce**, followed by the beech. The larch is a special conifer that turns golden in autumn and loses its needles. Famous wooden buildings are the Chapel Bridge in Lucerne and the old wooden houses in Valais and the Emmental.

Working with wood produces a lot of **sawdust**, on which Swiss wrestlers fight, for example. Wood chips are pressed into chipboard. Paper and cardboard are made from the wood fibres. Even bark and leftover wood are still used as fuel in wood-fired heating systems.

begriffe.erklaerung: The substance that plant cell walls are made of; it gives wood its tensile strength.
A wood substance that glues the cells together and makes the wood hard.
A ring in the cross-section of a trunk that shows one year’s growth.
A raw material that is formed again and again in nature.

gewusst: There are woods so dense that they sink in water, for example ebony.
The Chapel Bridge in Lucerne is regarded as one of the oldest covered wooden bridges in Europe.
A large part of wood consists of carbon that the tree has taken from the air.

teile.einleitung: Isotopes are different kinds of atoms of the same chemical element. They have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons in the nucleus. That is why they differ in weight but react almost the same way chemically.
wichtigste: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The word isotope comes from Greek and means “same place”.
Chemically, isotopes of an element hardly react differently.
Deuterium is hydrogen with one neutron; tritium has two neutrons.
Carbon-12 is the most common carbon isotope.
Carbon-14 is used to find out the age of finds.
Isotopes that decay and give off radiation are called radioactive isotopes.
In nuclear power stations, uranium-235 is split.

abschnitte.text: Every atom has an **atomic nucleus** made of protons and neutrons. The number of **protons** decides which element it is: hydrogen has one, carbon six, uranium 92. The number of **neutrons**, however, can vary. Atoms with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons are called isotopes. They are written with the mass number, for example carbon-12 with six neutrons and carbon-14 with eight neutrons.

The name comes from Greek: isos means “same” and topos means **“place”**. This is because isotopes are in the same place in the periodic table. The term was introduced by the British chemist Frederick Soddy in 1913. Studying radioactive substances, he had noticed that there are atoms that are chemically the same but differ in weight. Today several thousand different isotopes are known; most of them are unstable.

Hydrogen has three natural isotopes: normal hydrogen without a neutron, **deuterium** with one and **tritium** with two neutrons. Water containing deuterium is called heavy water and is about ten per cent heavier than normal water. Tritium is radioactive and is used, for example, in glowing watch hands. In nature, carbon consists of about 99 per cent carbon-12. A tiny part is radioactive carbon-14.

Some isotopes are unstable and decay over time, giving off **radiation**. They are called radioactive isotopes. The time it takes for half of the atoms to decay is called the **half-life**. For carbon-14 it is about 5730 years. Uranium-235 makes up only about 0.7 per cent of natural uranium and is split in nuclear power stations, as it used to be at Mühleberg and still is at Gösgen and Leibstadt.

The **radiocarbon method** is used to find the age of wood, bones or fabrics up to about 50,000 years old. It was developed around 1949 by the American Willard Libby, who received the Nobel Prize for it. In medicine, radioactive isotopes help to detect and treat diseases, for example iodine-131 for thyroid diseases. With stable isotopes, scientists can find out where a food comes from or what the climate was like long ago. The glacier mummy Ötzi was also dated with the radiocarbon method.

begriffe.erklaerung: A positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
An uncharged particle in the atomic nucleus.
The sum of protons and neutrons in an atomic nucleus.
The time after which half of the radioactive atoms have decayed.
The decay of unstable atomic nuclei, which produces radiation.

gewusst: Heavy water looks just like normal water, but an ice cube made from it sinks in normal water.
Tin has ten stable isotopes, more than any other element.
The age of the glacier mummy Ötzi, over 5000 years, was determined with carbon-14.

teile.einleitung: An ion is an atom or a group of atoms that is electrically charged. This happens when an atom gives up or takes up electrons. Ions are found in table salt, in seawater and even in our nerves.
wichtigste: Ions are electrically charged atoms or groups of atoms.
Positively charged ions are called cations, negatively charged ones anions.
Metals usually form cations, for example Na⁺ or Al³⁺.
There are also ions made of several atoms, such as sulphate SO₄²⁻ or ammonium NH₄⁺.
Table salt consists of sodium ions and chloride ions.
Molten salt conducts electricity because the ions can then move freely.
Ionisation energy is the energy needed to tear an electron away from an atom.

abschnitte.text: A normal atom has as many positive **protons** as negative electrons and is therefore neutral. If it gives up an electron, it becomes positively charged and is called a **cation**.
