If it takes up an electron, it becomes negatively charged and is called an **anion**. The energy needed to tear an electron away from an atom in the gas state is called **ionisation energy**.

Atoms like to form ions that have the same number of electrons as a noble gas, because this is particularly stable. Sodium gives up one electron and becomes Na⁺, which has as many electrons as **neon**. The two are said to be **isoelectronic**. Chlorine takes up one electron and becomes the chloride ion Cl⁻ with the electron number of argon.

Cations and anions attract each other strongly and form a regular **ionic lattice**. This is how a salt such as table salt, that is sodium chloride NaCl, is formed. An aluminium ion typically carries the charge 3+, a calcium ion the charge 2+. That is why the **empirical formula** of calcium chloride is CaCl₂, because two chloride ions balance one calcium ion.

Some ions consist of several firmly joined atoms; they are called **polyatomic ions**. The sulphate ion SO₄²⁻, for example, is found in gypsum. The ammonium ion NH₄⁺ is found in many fertilisers. The carbonate ion CO₃²⁻ is also important, because together with calcium it forms the limestone of the Alps.

Solid table salt does not conduct electricity, because the ions are fixed in the lattice. In **molten salt** or in salt water, the ions can move freely and carry charge. That is why tap water with dissolved salts is dangerous near electricity. Our body also needs ions: sodium and potassium make sure that signals travel along the **nerves**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A positively charged ion; it has given up electrons.
A negatively charged ion; it has taken up electrons.
The regular arrangement of ions in a salt crystal.
The energy needed to take an electron away from an atom.
Having the same number of electrons as another particle.

gewusst: The word ion comes from Greek and means “going” or “wandering”, because ions move in an electric current.
The name was introduced in 1834 by the English scientist Michael Faraday.
Sports drinks contain ions because you lose salts when you sweat.

teile.einleitung: Isomerism means that different substances are made of exactly the same atoms, but these are arranged differently. Such substances are called isomers; they have the same molecular formula but often completely different properties. You can compare it to Lego bricks: you can build different figures from the same bricks.
wichtigste: Isomers always have the same molecular formula.
For the formula C4H10 there are two isomers, n-butane and 2-methylpropane.
There are three structural isomers for C5H12 and five for C6H14.
Ethanol and dimethyl ether are isomers with the formula C2H6O.
Stereoisomers differ only in the arrangement of the atoms in space.
Because a C=C double bond cannot rotate freely, but-2-ene has a cis and a trans isomer.
In the E/Z naming system, Z stands for “zusammen” (together).

abschnitte.text: A **molecular formula** such as C4H10 only says how many atoms of which kind are in a molecule. But it does not reveal how the atoms are joined together. That is why there can be several different molecules for one molecular formula. These **isomers** often have different boiling points, smells or effects.

In **structural isomers** the atoms are joined in a different order. Butane can form a straight chain, which is n-butane, or a branched chain, which is 2-methylpropane. The more carbon atoms a molecule has, the more isomers there are: for C5H12 there are three, for C6H14 already five. A particularly clear example is ethanol, an alcohol, and dimethyl ether, a gas, which are both C2H6O.

Parts of a molecule can rotate freely around a single bond, but not around a **double bond**. That is why two identical groups can lie on the same side of the double bond, which is the **cis form**, or on opposite sides, which is the trans form. In but-2-ene there are thus two different substances. In the newer E/Z naming system, Z stands for the German “zusammen” (together) and E for “entgegen” (opposite).

Some molecules behave like our left and right hands: they are mirror images but cannot be laid exactly on top of each other. Such molecules are called **chiral**, and the two forms are called **enantiomers**. Our nose can sometimes tell them apart. The substance carvone smells of mint in one form and of caraway in the other.

At the beginning of the 19th century chemists believed that the same composition also meant the same substance. Then Friedrich Wöhler and Justus von Liebig found two substances with the same composition but different properties. In 1830 the Swede Jöns Jakob Berzelius gave this phenomenon the name **isomerism**. In 1848 Louis Pasteur separated mirror-image crystals from each other under the microscope for the first time.

In our body many substances fit like a key in a lock, and only the right isomer fits. That is why with medicines one form can heal while the other has no effect. Glucose and fructose are also isomers with the formula C6H12O6, but they taste differently sweet. Chemists must therefore know exactly which **isomer** they are making.

begriffe.erklaerung: Different substances with the same molecular formula but a different structure.
A formula that shows how many atoms of each kind a molecule contains.
Isomers whose atoms are joined in a different order.
Isomers with the same connections but a different arrangement in space.
Handed, that is mirror images like a left and right hand that cannot be laid exactly on top of each other.

gewusst: For the molecular formula C20H42 there are over 300,000 different structural isomers.
The two mirror-image forms of carvone smell of spearmint chewing gum in one case and of caraway in the other.
Glucose and fructose are made of exactly the same atoms.

teile.einleitung: The ionic bond is one of the ways in which atoms hold together firmly. One atom gives up electrons and another takes them up; this creates positively and negatively charged particles that attract each other. All salts are built up in this way, for example our table salt.
wichtigste: An ionic bond typically forms between metal and non-metal atoms.
Electrostatic attraction holds the oppositely charged ions together.
A positively charged ion is called a cation, a negatively charged ion an anion.
A magnesium atom that gives up two outer electrons becomes the ion Mg²⁺.
A sulphide ion carries the charge 2-.
In a solid salt, the ions are arranged in a regular ionic lattice.
If struck hard, salt crystals shatter instead of changing shape.

abschnitte.text: Metal atoms such as sodium have only a few electrons in their outermost shell and give them up easily. Non-metal atoms such as chlorine, on the other hand, readily take up electrons. If sodium gives its outer electron to chlorine, both have a stable **noble gas configuration**. The atoms have thus become charged particles, the **ions**.

An atom that gives up electrons becomes positively charged and is called a **cation**, for example Na⁺ or Mg²⁺. An atom that takes up electrons becomes negative and is called an **anion**, for example Cl⁻ or O²⁻. Plus and minus attract each other like the poles of magnets. This **electrostatic attraction** is the ionic bond itself.

In a salt crystal, countless ions arrange themselves alternately in a regular **ionic lattice**. In table salt, each sodium ion is surrounded by six chloride ions and vice versa. That is why grains of salt look like little cubes under a magnifying glass. The formula only gives the ratio of numbers; for magnesium oxide made of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ it is therefore MgO.

Ionic compounds have very high melting points; table salt only melts at about 800 °C. They are hard but **brittle**: when struck, the layers shift, ions with the same charge end up next to each other and repel each other. As solids, salts do not conduct electricity. When molten or dissolved in water, however, they conduct well, because the ions can then move freely.

Table salt is sodium chloride, that is Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Limestone consists of calcium ions and carbonate ions. Gypsum, road salt and many minerals in rock are also **ionic compounds**. Mineral water contains dissolved ions such as calcium and magnesium, which are listed on the label.

Whether an ionic bond forms depends on how strongly the atoms attract electrons. This measure is called **electronegativity**. If the difference between two atoms is large, an ionic bond forms. If it is small, the atoms prefer to share the electrons, and then it is called a covalent bond.

begriffe.erklaerung: An electrically charged particle formed from an atom by giving up or taking up electrons.
A positively charged ion.
A negatively charged ion.
A regular three-dimensional arrangement of ions in a solid salt.
A measure of how strongly an atom pulls electrons towards itself.

gewusst: Sodium is a violently reacting metal and chlorine a poisonous gas; together they make harmless table salt.
Salt water conducts electricity much better than pure water, because ions move in it.

teile.einleitung: In chemistry, an indicator is a substance that shows by its colour whether a solution is acidic or alkaline. You can even find some indicators in the kitchen, for example in red cabbage juice. Chemists use indicators to check acidity quickly and easily.
wichtigste: An indicator shows by its colour whether a solution is acidic or alkaline.
Litmus is obtained from lichens and is violet in a neutral solution.
Red cabbage juice turns red with vinegar and green to yellow in a strongly alkaline solution.
Phenolphthalein turns pink to violet in an alkali.
The hydrangea flowers blue or pink depending on how acidic the soil is.
Black tea gets lighter with lemon juice because its pigments act as an indicator.
Universal indicators show the approximate pH with many colours.

abschnitte.text: The word **indicator** comes from the Latin indicare, which means “to show”. An acid-base indicator is a dye that changes colour when the **pH** changes. The pH usually ranges from 0 to 14: below 7 a solution is acidic, at 7 neutral and above 7 **basic** or alkaline. An indicator changes its colour within a particular pH range, the transition range. So you can see at a glance whether lemon juice, soapy water or tap water is acidic or alkaline.

**Litmus** is one of the oldest indicators and is obtained from certain **lichens**. It turns red in acids, blue in alkalis and violet in neutral solutions. In the laboratory, people often use litmus paper, which is dipped briefly into the liquid. This is also where the expression “litmus test” for a decisive check comes from. Litmus only shows roughly whether something is acidic or alkaline.

The juice of **red cabbage** contains pigments called anthocyanins. If you add vinegar, the juice turns red; in water it stays violet, and in soapy water it turns blue to green. In strongly alkaline solutions it even turns yellow. Black tea is also an indicator: it gets lighter with lemon juice. Blueberry juice and red onions show similar colour changes.

**Phenolphthalein** is colourless in acidic and neutral solutions and turns pink to violet in alkalis. Methyl orange changes from red to yellowish orange in the acidic range. A **universal indicator** is a mixture of several dyes and shows many different colours for different pH values. In a titration, acid or alkali is added drop by drop until the indicator changes colour. Today the pH is also often measured electronically with a pH meter.

The **hydrangea** is a garden plant whose flowers turn blue on acidic soils and pink on chalky, alkaline soils. The reason is that the plant can take up more aluminium in acidic soil, which changes the colour of the flowers. Gardeners make use of this to grow blue hydrangeas. Many flower colours in roses, violets or cornflowers also come from anthocyanins. In schools in Switzerland, the red cabbage experiment is a popular first chemistry experiment.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number from 0 to 14 that shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is.
The opposite of acidic; also called alkaline.
An indicator from lichens, red in acid and blue in alkali.
Red, violet and blue plant pigments, for example in red cabbage.
A method for finding out the exact amount of an acid or alkali.

gewusst: With red cabbage juice you can make a whole rainbow scale of colours at home.
The expression “litmus test” is also used for decisive checks outside chemistry.
In some regions red cabbage is called “Blaukraut” (blue cabbage) in German, because it turns bluish when cooked with alkaline water.

teile.einleitung: The law of definite proportions is a basic rule of chemistry. It states that a chemical compound always contains its elements in the same ratio by mass. Whether water comes from the Alps or from the laboratory, it is always made up in the same way.
wichtigste: A compound always contains its elements in the same ratio by mass.
The law was formulated at the end of the 18th century by the Frenchman Joseph-Louis Proust.
In water, hydrogen and oxygen are in a ratio of about 1 to 8.
So 3 g of hydrogen react with 24 g of oxygen.
A mixture such as salt water can vary, but the compound sodium chloride has a fixed composition.
Compounds with a variable composition are called berthollides.
John Dalton’s atomic theory explained the law.

abschnitte.text: The law says: in a pure **compound**, the masses of the elements involved are always in the same **ratio**. Water, for example, always contains about 1 gram of hydrogen for every 8 grams of oxygen. So if you want to make water, exactly 24 grams of oxygen react with 3 grams of hydrogen. If more oxygen is present, the rest is simply left over.

With the law you can calculate amounts as in a **rule of three** problem. 24 g of magnesium combine with 16 g of oxygen to form 40 g of magnesium oxide. If you take only 12 g of magnesium, that is half, you get 20 g of magnesium oxide. In copper(II) sulphide, 6.35 g of copper go with 3.21 g of sulphur, so 19.05 g of copper go with three times as much, namely 9.63 g of sulphur.

At the end of the 18th century the French chemist **Joseph-Louis Proust** examined many substances very precisely. He found that copper carbonate, for example, always has the same composition, no matter where it comes from. His fellow countryman **Claude-Louis Berthollet**, on the other hand, believed that compounds could form in any ratios. The dispute lasted for years; in the end Proust largely won.

Why the law holds was explained by the Englishman **John Dalton** at the beginning of the 19th century with his **atomic theory**. Every element consists of atoms with a particular mass. In a compound, the atoms combine in fixed number ratios, for example two hydrogen atoms with one oxygen atom. That is why the ratio by mass is always the same too.

The law helps to tell **compounds** apart from mixtures. Salt water is a mixture, because you can dissolve more or less salt in it. Sodium chloride, that is table salt itself, on the other hand always has the same composition. There are exceptions, however, such as certain iron oxides like wüstite, which are called **berthollides** in honour of Berthollet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A pure substance in which different elements are firmly joined chemically.
Different substances that are only mixed and not chemically joined.
How many grams of one substance go with how many grams of another.
A compound with a slightly variable composition.

gewusst: The law of definite proportions helped to prove the existence of atoms long before they could be seen.
A water molecule from a glacier is made up in exactly the same way as one from the tap.
Proust worked in Spain for a time, where he carried out many of his investigations.

teile.einleitung: Ketones are a group of organic substances that all have a special group of atoms: a carbon atom with a double-bonded oxygen that is attached to two other carbon atoms. The best-known ketone is acetone, which is found in many nail varnish removers.
wichtigste: Ketones contain a carbonyl group, that is a carbon atom with a double bond to an oxygen atom.
In ketones the carbonyl carbon atom is bonded to two other carbon atoms, so a ketone needs at least three carbon atoms.
The simplest ketone is called propanone according to IUPAC; better known is the name acetone.
The ketone with four carbon atoms is called butanone.
Ketones are formed when secondary alcohols are oxidised.
Ketones give a negative result in Fehling’s test.
Ketones and their enol form are in equilibrium with each other in keto-enol tautomerism.

abschnitte.text: All ketones have the **carbonyl group** C=O. In ketones this group is always in the middle of a carbon chain, because the carbonyl carbon atom has a carbon group on its left and on its right. If, on the other hand, the carbonyl group is at the end of the chain, it is called an aldehyde. According to the IUPAC rules, ketones are given the ending **-one**, for example propanone or butanone.

**Acetone** or propanone is a colourless, highly flammable liquid with a typical smell. It dissolves fats, varnishes and many plastics and is therefore used as nail varnish remover and as a solvent. Acetone mixes with water in any ratio. Industry produces millions of tonnes of acetone every year, mainly as a starting material for plastics.

If you oxidise a secondary alcohol, such as propan-2-ol, a ketone is formed. Ketones are hard to oxidise any further, which is why **Fehling’s test** and the silver mirror test are negative for them. This is how ketones can be told apart from aldehydes in the laboratory. Ketones can also exist in a form with a C=C double bond and an OH group, the enol; this is called **keto-enol tautomerism**.

The carbonyl group is polar, which is why small ketones dissolve well in water. Acetone boils at 56 °C, lower than the similarly sized alcohol propan-2-ol at 82 °C. The reason: acetone molecules cannot form **hydrogen bonds** with each other, because they lack a hydrogen atom on an oxygen atom. With water, however, they can form hydrogen bonds.

abschnitte.titel: Ketones in nature and the body
abschnitte.text: Many ketones occur in nature. The fruit sugar fructose has a keto group, as do the fragrance camphor and the hormone cortisone. When the body fasts for a long time and breaks down fat, the liver forms so-called ketone bodies, one of which is acetone. That is why the breath can then smell slightly of acetone.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of atoms made of a carbon atom with a double bond to an oxygen atom.
The simplest ketone, chemically propanone, known from nail varnish remover.
An alcohol in which the carbon atom with the OH group is bonded to two other carbon atoms.
An equilibrium between two forms of a molecule that differ by a moving hydrogen atom.

gewusst: The word ketone was derived from the name acetone in the 19th century.
Butanone is also called methyl ethyl ketone and is a common solvent in glues.
The human body also makes small amounts of acetone itself.

teile.einleitung: A boiled egg is a classic on the breakfast table and at Easter. But something amazing happens when it is cooked: the clear, runny egg white turns white and firm. This change is chemical and can never be reversed.
wichtigste: When cooked, the egg white turns white and firm.
The egg white sets first, then the yolk.
A hard-boiled egg is cooked for about 10 minutes.
A boiled egg can never be made raw again.
After cooking, eggs are put in cold water so that they stop cooking.
Eggs boiled for too long get a greenish ring around the yolk.
A hard-boiled egg spins quickly and evenly on the table.

abschnitte.titel: What happens when you boil an egg?
abschnitte.text: The egg white, also called **albumen**, consists mainly of water and **proteins**. Proteins are long, intricately folded molecules. The heat makes them unfold and clump together into a firm network. This process is called **denaturation** or coagulation. The network scatters the light, which is why the previously clear egg white turns white.

The heat travels from the outside inwards, so the egg white sets first and the yolk only later. After about 4 to 5 minutes in boiling water an egg is soft-boiled: the white is firm, the yolk still runny. After about 6 to 7 minutes the yolk is jammy. For a hard-boiled egg, allow about 10 minutes. Large eggs and eggs straight from the fridge need a little longer.

At the blunt end of every egg there is a small **air cell**. When heated, the air expands and can crack the shell, which is why eggs are often pricked before boiling. After boiling, the eggs are plunged into cold water so that they stop cooking. In the mountains water boils below 100 degrees, at 3000 metres at about 90 degrees. So eggs take longer there.

If you boil an egg far too long, the yolk gets a greenish grey ring. Sulphur is released from the egg white, and iron from the yolk. The two combine to form **iron sulphide**, which looks greenish. The egg is still edible, but it often tastes a little of sulphur. Cooling it in time prevents the green ring.

With a simple test you can tell a boiled egg from a raw one: you spin it on the table. A hard-boiled egg is solid inside and spins quickly and evenly. In a raw egg the liquid sloshes about and slows the spin, so the egg wobbles slowly. If you stop a raw egg briefly with your finger, it often keeps turning a little afterwards because the inside is still moving.

A hen’s egg provides valuable proteins, vitamins and minerals. In Switzerland, boiled eggs are traditionally dyed and hidden at **Easter**. In “Eiertütschen”, two people knock the tips of their eggs against each other; whoever’s egg stays whole wins. Boiled, unpeeled eggs keep for a few days in the fridge, and dyed Easter eggs without cracks often even longer.

begriffe.erklaerung: A change in proteins caused by heat or acid, in which they lose their shape and become firm.
An important building block of living things and a nutrient.
The clear part of the egg around the yolk, also called albumen.
A small space filled with air at the blunt end of the egg.
To cool something hot quickly with cold water.

gewusst: The older an egg is, the easier it is to peel after boiling.
A fresh raw egg sinks in water; a very old egg can stand upright or float because its air cell has grown larger.
When frying an egg, the egg white also denaturates, only through the heat of the pan instead of water.

teile.einleitung: A sewage treatment plant cleans the dirty water from homes, schools and factories before it flows back into rivers and lakes. In Switzerland it is usually called an ARA, which stands for “Abwasserreinigungsanlage” (waste water treatment plant). Screens, tanks and billions of tiny bacteria help with the work.
wichtigste: A sewage treatment plant cleans waste water.
In Switzerland it is often abbreviated to ARA.
The water from the toilet flows through the sewers to the treatment plant.
A screen at the entrance holds back large objects.
Tiny bacteria eat the dirt in the water.
In the digester, biogas is produced from sludge.
The cleaned water flows into a river or lake, and in Switzerland the sewage sludge is burnt.

abschnitte.text: Everything we flush down the washbasin, shower and toilet flows through underground pipes, the **sewers**. In many places rainwater from roads and roofs is added too. In the end the waste water reaches the treatment plant. There it is cleaned in several stages, which often takes about a day.

First a **screen** holds back large objects such as cotton buds, wet wipes and plastic. In the grit chamber, sand and small stones sink to the bottom. Then the water flows slowly through the **primary settling tank**, where more dirt particles settle as sludge. Fat floats on top and is skimmed off.

In the **aeration tank**, billions of bacteria and other tiny organisms are at work. They eat the dissolved dirt in the water and multiply as they do so. So that they get enough oxygen, air is blown into the tank. In the secondary settling tank the flakes of bacteria sink, and the water at the top is now clean.

Iron salts are used to remove **phosphate** from the water, which would otherwise make too many algae grow in lakes. Many large Swiss treatment plants also have a fourth stage with ozone or activated carbon. It removes **micropollutants**, that is tiny residues of medicines, pesticides and cosmetics. Switzerland was one of the first countries to make this extra treatment compulsory.

The settled sludge goes into the **digester**, a large closed tank. There bacteria break down the sludge without oxygen, and biogas is produced. With the gas, the treatment plant generates electricity and heat for its own operation. In Switzerland the remaining sewage sludge may no longer be spread on fields; it is burnt.

abschnitte.titel: Clean lakes thanks to the ARA
abschnitte.text: In the 1960s many Swiss rivers and lakes were badly polluted, and in some places swimming was banned. Only after that were treatment plants built almost everywhere. Today nearly every house in Switzerland is connected to an **ARA**. That is why people can swim in the Aare, the Rhine or Lake Zurich again today.

begriffe.erklaerung: Short for “Abwasserreinigungsanlage”, the Swiss word for sewage treatment plant.
A network of underground pipes that collects and carries away waste water.
A tank in which bacteria clean the water with the help of air.
A closed tank in which biogas is produced from sewage sludge.
Tiny residues of medicines or chemicals in water.

gewusst: Cotton buds, wet wipes and food leftovers belong in the bin and not in the toilet, because they can block pumps.
A large treatment plant can cover a considerable part of its electricity needs itself with biogas.
Invisible to people and animals, millions of bacteria are at work in a single drop of activated sludge.

teile.einleitung: Iodised salt is table salt to which a small amount of iodine has been added. We need iodine for the thyroid gland, but there is too little of it in Swiss soils and food. That is why Switzerland was one of the first countries in the world to introduce iodised salt.
wichtigste: Iodised salt is table salt with a small addition of iodine.
The thyroid gland needs iodine to make important hormones.
In the past, goitre was common in Switzerland because of iodine deficiency.
In 1922 Switzerland was one of the first countries with iodised salt.
Swiss soils have little iodine because glaciers and rain have washed it away.
Sea fish naturally contains a lot of iodine.
Heated iodine forms violet vapour.

abschnitte.text: **Iodised salt** is normal table salt to which a tiny amount of an iodine compound is added. You cannot taste the addition. In Switzerland, iodised salt today contains about 25 milligrams of iodine per kilogram of salt. The salt comes from the **Swiss Saltworks**, which extract it from the ground at Rheinfelden, Riburg and Bex. Most bakeries also use iodised salt, so iodine gets into our diet through bread.

The **thyroid gland** is a small organ in the neck shaped like a butterfly. It makes **hormones** that control metabolism, growth and the development of the brain. It needs iodine for these hormones. If there is not enough iodine, the thyroid gland grows larger to capture more of it. This visible swelling in the neck is called a **goitre**.

During the Ice Age, glaciers removed the top layer of soil, and rain washed out the iodine over thousands of years. That is why Swiss soils and the plants growing on them contain little iodine. In the past, a great many people in some Alpine valleys had a goitre. With severe iodine deficiency, children were also born with developmental disorders. In 1922 the canton of **Appenzell Ausserrhoden** was the first to introduce iodised salt; other cantons soon followed, and goitre became rare.

There is a lot of iodine in **sea fish** such as cod or coley and in seaweed. Milk and eggs also contain some iodine. Anyone in Switzerland who hardly eats fish depends on iodised salt. Experts recommend choosing iodised salt when salting food at home, but not eating too much salt overall. By the way, sea salt does not automatically contain a lot of iodine.

Iodine is a chemical element from the group of **halogens**. Pure iodine forms shiny greyish black crystals. If you heat them, a beautiful **violet vapour** forms, which is where the name comes from: the Greek word for “violet-coloured”. Iodine was discovered in 1811 by the Frenchman Bernard Courtois in the ash of seaweed. In the past, wounds were disinfected with **tincture of iodine**, and if you drip iodine solution onto a potato, the starch in it turns bluish black.

begriffe.erklaerung: A butterfly-shaped organ in the neck that makes hormones.
An enlargement of the thyroid gland, often caused by iodine deficiency.
A chemical messenger that controls processes in the body.
A group of elements that includes iodine, chlorine and fluorine.
A nutrient in potatoes and grain that turns bluish black with iodine.

gewusst: Iodine is one of the few elements that can change directly from solid to gas when heated.
A person needs only about 150 micrograms of iodine a day, which is just 0.15 milligrams.
Switzerland is regarded worldwide as a pioneer in fighting iodine deficiency with salt.

teile.einleitung: Glass is a transparent, hard material that is made mainly from sand. The raw materials are melted at over 1000 degrees and the melt is left to solidify. Windows, bottles, spectacles and even the fibres that carry internet data are made of glass.
wichtigste: Glass is made mainly from sand.
Melting it requires temperatures of over 1000 degrees.
Glass that is heated very strongly becomes soft and can be shaped.
A glassblower uses a pipe to shape hot glass into vases and vessels.
Glass is hard but brittle and easily breaks into sharp pieces.
Behind the glass of a mirror there is a thin layer of metal.
In Switzerland, waste glass is collected separately by colour and recycled.

abschnitte.text: The most important raw material is **quartz sand**, which consists mainly of silicon dioxide. Soda is added so that the sand melts at a lower temperature, and lime so that the glass becomes firm and durable. This mixture is melted at over 1000 degrees, in industry usually at around 1500 degrees. As it cools, the particles do not form an ordered lattice: glass is **amorphous**, a solidified melt.

Glass is transparent, hard and does not rust. It hardly reacts with food, which is why it is well suited for bottles and jars. At the same time it is **brittle**: if a drinking glass falls on a hard floor, it breaks into sharp pieces, which you should never pick up with your bare hands. If glass is heated strongly, it slowly becomes soft instead of suddenly turning liquid.

A **glassblower** uses a long tube, the blowpipe, to pick up a ball of glowing glass and blows it up. This is how vases, bowls and Christmas tree baubles are made. Window glass today is usually made as **float glass**, by letting liquid glass solidify completely flat and smooth on a bath of liquid tin. At the Glasi Hergiswil in the canton of Nidwalden you can watch glassblowers at work.

People made the first glass objects several thousand years ago in Mesopotamia and Egypt, first beads and small vessels. Around the time of the Romans, glassblowing with a pipe was invented, and glass thus became an everyday product. In the Middle Ages, colourful stained glass windows decorated churches. Today there are special glasses for screens, laboratory equipment and **optical fibres**, which carry light and data over long distances.

Window panes, spectacle lenses, marbles, drinking glasses and mirrors are made of glass. Behind the glass, a mirror has a thin layer of silver or aluminium that reflects the light. Waste glass can be melted down again and again without getting worse. In Switzerland it is collected separately by the colours clear, brown and green, and a very large part of it is recycled.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fine sand that consists mainly of silicon dioxide.
Without an ordered lattice; the particles lie in disorder as in a liquid.
Breaks suddenly instead of bending.
A very thin thread of glass that carries light and data.

gewusst: Glass also forms in nature, for example as obsidian from volcanic lava or when lightning strikes sand.
The fact that old church windows are thicker at the bottom is not because glass flows, but because of the way they were made at the time.
Waste glass can be melted down as often as you like and made into new bottles.

teile.einleitung: A catalyst is a substance that makes a chemical reaction run faster without being used up itself. It works like a short-cut tunnel through a mountain: the destination stays the same, but the route becomes easier. Catalysts clean car exhaust, help with the production of fertiliser and work as enzymes in our body.
wichtigste: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up.
It lowers the activation energy of a reaction.
A catalyst does not change the total energy released.
The catalytic converter in a car turns poisonous carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide.
In many catalytic converters, the precious metal platinum does the work.
Catalysts in living things are called enzymes.
In the Haber-Bosch process, ammonia is made with an iron catalyst.

abschnitte.text: For a reaction to start, it needs a push of energy, the **activation energy**. You can imagine it as a mountain that the substances must get over. A catalyst opens up a different route with a lower mountain, rather like a tunnel through the Alps. That is why the substances react faster, but in the end the same products form with the same energy balance.

The catalyst takes part in the reaction, but is released again at the end. That is why a small amount is often enough to convert a great deal of substance. A nice school experiment is **manganese dioxide** in hydrogen peroxide: it foams vigorously because oxygen is released. The manganese dioxide then lies unchanged in the glass.

In the exhaust of many cars there is a **catalytic converter** with a honeycomb structure coated with platinum, palladium or rhodium. It turns poisonous carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide. It also turns nitrogen oxides into harmless nitrogen and burns up remains of fuel. In Switzerland catalytic converters were introduced in the 1980s to make the air cleaner.

In living things too, chemical reactions are taking place all the time that would be far too slow without help. This is the job of **enzymes**, the catalysts of life. The **amylase** in saliva starts breaking starch down into sugar already in the mouth. That is why bread tastes sweetish if you chew it for a long time.

Most chemical products are made with catalysts today. In the **Haber-Bosch process**, ammonia is formed from nitrogen and hydrogen with an iron catalyst. From it, artificial fertiliser is made, which feeds a great many people worldwide. Plastics, fuels and margarine are also produced with the help of catalysts.

In 1835 the Swedish chemist Jöns Jakob Berzelius coined the term **catalysis**. The word comes from Greek and means roughly “loosening”. The German Wilhelm Ostwald researched how catalysts work and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1909. Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch later also received Nobel Prizes for their work.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
Energy needed for a reaction to start at all.
A protein that acts as a catalyst in the body.
Speeding up a chemical reaction with a catalyst.

gewusst: Without enzymes, digesting a meal would take many years.
About half of the nitrogen in our body comes from fertiliser made with the Haber-Bosch process.
A catalytic converter only works properly once it is a few hundred degrees hot.

teile.einleitung: Glucose, also known in everyday life as dextrose or grape sugar, is the most important sugar in nature. Plants make it with sunlight, and our body uses it as a fast source of energy for muscles and brain. Its name comes from the Greek word glykys, which means “sweet”.
wichtigste: Glucose has the molecular formula C6H12O6.
In everyday life glucose is called dextrose; it tastes a little less sweet than table sugar.
Glucose is a carbohydrate and a simple sugar.
Table sugar, sucrose, consists of glucose and fructose.
In Fehling’s test, glucose forms a brick-red precipitate.
Without oxygen, yeast ferments glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide.
The hormone insulin lowers the amount of glucose in the blood.

abschnitte.text: Glucose is a **simple sugar**, that is a carbohydrate made of only one sugar unit. Its molecule consists of 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 6 oxygen atoms; the formula is C6H12O6. It is found in grapes, other fruit and honey, hence the name **grape sugar**. You can buy it in any shop as a white powder or in tablets. It tastes a little less sweet than ordinary table sugar.

Plants produce glucose during **photosynthesis**. Using the energy of sunlight, they turn carbon dioxide from the air and water into glucose and oxygen. They link the glucose into long chains: into **starch** as a store, for example in potatoes and grain, and into cellulose, the building material of wood and plant fibres. Glucose is thus the basis of almost all food chains on Earth.

In the body, starch from bread, pasta or rice is broken down into glucose, which passes from the gut into the blood. The cells burn it with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water and gain energy in this way. The brain depends particularly on glucose. The body stores surplus glucose as **glycogen** in the liver and muscles. Because dextrose does not have to be digested first, it goes into the blood very quickly.

The amount of glucose in the blood is called **blood sugar** and is closely controlled by the body. If it rises after a meal, the pancreas releases the hormone **insulin**, which helps the cells take up glucose. If it falls too low, the hormone glucagon makes sure that glucose is released from the glycogen store. In the disease diabetes, this control does not work properly, and those affected have to measure their blood sugar regularly.

Glucose can be detected with **Fehling’s test**: you heat it with a blue copper solution, and a brick-red precipitate forms. Without oxygen, yeasts ferment glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide. This **fermentation** is used in baking bread, where the gas makes the dough rise. It also plays a part in making wine and beer.

Our table sugar is chemically called **sucrose** and is a double sugar made of glucose and fructose. In Switzerland it is obtained from sugar beet, in the sugar factories at Aarberg and Frauenfeld. Experts advise not eating too much added sugar, for example in sugary drinks. Too much sugar can cause tooth decay and increase the risk of being overweight.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sugar made of only one unit, for example glucose or fructose.
A group of nutrients that includes sugar, starch and cellulose.
The storage form of glucose in the liver and muscles.
A hormone from the pancreas that lowers blood sugar.
The breakdown of sugar by yeasts or bacteria without oxygen.

gewusst: A single starch grain from a potato consists of countless glucose units linked together.
If you chew a piece of bread for a long time, it tastes sweet, because saliva breaks starch down into sugar.
The paper of a book also consists mostly of glucose, namely of cellulose, which is built from long glucose chains.

teile.einleitung: Lime, in the everyday sense, means calcium carbonate, a white substance found in rock, shells and eggshells. Whole mountain ranges such as the Jura consist mostly of limestone. At home we know it as limescale, the annoying white layer in the kettle.
wichtigste: Chemically, it is calcium carbonate with the formula CaCO3.
The Jura mountains consist mostly of limestone.
Mussel shells, snail shells and eggshells consist mainly of calcium carbonate.
In the sea, corals build huge reefs out of calcium carbonate.
Stalactites and stalagmites in caves are made of calcium carbonate.
Tap water with a lot of dissolved calcium carbonate is called hard water.
If you drip vinegar onto limestone, it fizzes because carbon dioxide is produced.

abschnitte.text: It is a compound of calcium, carbon and oxygen that chemists call **calcium carbonate**. It is white, rather soft and hardly dissolves in pure water. Depending on how it formed, it occurs as limestone, chalk or marble. Marble is limestone that has been transformed deep in the Earth by heat and pressure.

Many sea creatures build their shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate, for example mussels, snails and **corals**. When they die, their remains sink to the sea floor. Over millions of years they are pressed together and become **limestone**. That is why fossilised shells and ammonites are often found in the limestone of the Jura and the Alps.

The whole **Jura** is built of limestone that formed in a sea about 150 million years ago. Many mountains in the Prealps, such as the Säntis or Pilatus, are also made of limestone. Rainwater slowly dissolves limestone and forms caves, sinkholes and underground rivers. The Hölloch in the Muotathal in the canton of Schwyz is one of the longest caves in the world, with more than 200 kilometres of passages.

When water flows through limestone, it dissolves some calcium carbonate and carries it along. When this water drips from the ceiling in a cave, the calcium carbonate is deposited again very slowly, and this is how **stalactites and stalagmites** form. Our tap water also contains dissolved calcium carbonate; a lot of it makes the water **hard**. When it is heated, the calcium carbonate settles as a layer of limescale in the kettle or coffee machine.

Calcium carbonate reacts with acids; it foams and fizzes because the gas **carbon dioxide** is produced. That is why you can remove limescale stains with vinegar or citric acid. Geologists recognise limestone by putting a drop of dilute hydrochloric acid on it. Acid rain also attacks monuments made of limestone and marble.

If you heat limestone to about 900 °C, carbon dioxide escapes and **quicklime** is formed. With water it becomes slaked lime, which mixed with sand gives a mortar. In the air this takes up carbon dioxide again and becomes as hard as stone. Limestone is also the most important raw material for cement.

begriffe.erklaerung: The chemical name of limestone, with the formula CaCO3.
Water with a lot of dissolved calcium carbonate and magnesium.
A column or icicle of calcium carbonate that grows in caves from dripping water.
A white powder produced by strongly heating limestone.

gewusst: The White Cliffs of Dover in England consist of chalk, that is the tiny calcium carbonate shells of sea creatures.
A stalactite often grows only about one centimetre in a hundred years.
A hen’s eggshell consists of about 95 per cent calcium carbonate.

teile.einleitung: Barbecue charcoal is charcoal that gives a hot, even glow when you have a barbecue. It is made when wood is strongly heated without much air. To make barbecuing fun, you need to know a few safety rules.
wichtigste: Barbecue charcoal is made from wood.
People who make charcoal are called charcoal burners.
Charcoal burners make charcoal in a large pile of wood, the charcoal kiln.
The charcoal is ready when it is covered with grey ash.
To light it you use firelighters and never methylated spirits or petrol.
A charcoal barbecue must never burn indoors, because a poisonous gas is produced.
Sausages are turned with barbecue tongs.

abschnitte.text: Barbecue charcoal is **charcoal**, that is wood that consists almost only of carbon. It is black, light and breaks easily. When it burns it gives off a lot of heat, but hardly any flames and little smoke. Besides pieces of charcoal there are **briquettes**, which are pressed blocks of charcoal powder. Briquettes burn longer and more evenly, but take more time to light.

abschnitte.titel: The charcoal burner and his kiln
abschnitte.text: Charcoal is made when wood is heated to several hundred degrees without much air getting in. The wood does not burn; instead water and other substances escape as gases. In the past, **charcoal burners** did this in a **charcoal kiln**, a large pile of wood covered with earth. A kiln glows for several days, and the charcoal burner has to watch it day and night. In Switzerland this old craft is still practised today in the Entlebuch, for example in Romoos. Today most barbecue charcoal is made in factories in large ovens.

To light it, you put **firelighters** between the charcoal or use a chimney starter. You must never use methylated spirits or petrol, especially not on charcoal that is already glowing, because a dangerous jet of flame can shoot up. It often takes about half an hour for the charcoal to be ready. You can tell because it is covered with a fine layer of **grey ash** and no longer has flames. Only then do you put sausages, vegetables or meat on the grill.

Burning charcoal produces **carbon monoxide**, a gas that you can neither see nor smell and that is very poisonous. That is why a charcoal barbecue must never be used in a flat, a tent or a garage, not even for heating. Children should always keep their distance from the hot barbecue. Sausages are turned with long **barbecue tongs** so that you do not burn yourself. The embers stay hot for many hours and should only go in the bin once they have cooled down completely.

A large part of the barbecue charcoal sold in Switzerland comes from abroad. Sometimes trees from tropical forests are cut down for it, which harms the forests. An **FSC label** on the packet shows that the wood comes from responsibly managed forests. Charcoal from Switzerland or neighbouring countries also has shorter transport routes. If you like, you can also light a fireplace with wood from the forest and wait until there is a nice bed of embers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Strongly heated wood that consists almost only of carbon.
A craftsman who makes charcoal from wood.
A large, covered pile of wood in which wood turns into charcoal.
An invisible, odourless and very poisonous gas.
A pressed block of charcoal powder.

gewusst: Charcoal is much lighter than the wood it was made from.
As early as the Stone Age, people painted animals on cave walls with charcoal.
In the past, a great deal of charcoal was needed to smelt iron from ore.

teile.einleitung: The ideal gas is a model that makes it easy to describe and calculate how gases behave. You imagine the gas particles as tiny points that fly about and do not attract one another. With the equation p · V = n · R · T, the pressure, volume and temperature of a gas can be calculated.
wichtigste: The ideal gas is a simplified model of gases.
In the model, the particles are points and do not attract one another.
The equation of state is p · V = n · R · T.
The universal gas constant R is about 8.314 J/(mol·K).
If you compress a gas to a third at the same temperature, the pressure triples.
Real gases behave almost ideally at high temperature and low pressure.
In 1873 Johannes Diderik van der Waals put forward an equation for real gases.

abschnitte.text: A gas consists of countless tiny particles that constantly fly about in all directions and bump against the walls of their container. In an **ideal gas** you imagine that these particles have no size of their own, so they are **points**. In addition, they do not attract each other and only collide like billiard balls. Such a gas does not exist in reality. But the model is so good that it can be used to calculate air, helium or nitrogen in everyday life quite accurately.

The **equation of state** is p · V = n · R · T. Here p is the pressure, V the volume, n the amount of substance in moles and T the temperature in kelvin. R is the **universal gas constant**, about 8.314 J/(mol·K). The temperature must always be given in **kelvin**; 0 kelvin corresponds to minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. At 0 °C and normal air pressure, one mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres.

If you compress a gas at the same temperature to a third of its volume, the pressure becomes three times as great. If you heat a gas at the same pressure from 27 °C to 327 °C, the temperature rises from 300 to 600 kelvin, and the volume doubles. One mole of gas in a 10-litre container at 300 kelvin exerts a pressure of about 249 kPa. That is about two and a half times normal air pressure. Calculations like these are needed all the time in chemistry, physics and engineering.

The equation combines several older **gas laws**. In the 17th century Robert Boyle and Edme Mariotte found that pressure and volume are inversely related at the same temperature. Around 1802 Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac showed that gases expand evenly when heated. In 1811 Amedeo Avogadro realised that equal volumes of gas contain the same number of particles. In 1873 **Johannes Diderik van der Waals** put forward an improved equation for real gases that takes into account the size and attraction of the particles.

A hot-air balloon rises because the heated air expands and so becomes lighter than the cold air outside. Bicycle tyres have less pressure in cold winter than in summer. You must never heat a spray can, because the pressure inside rises sharply and it can burst. When you pump up a tyre, the air in the pump is compressed and gets warm. At very high pressure or low temperature the model no longer fits well, and then gases even turn liquid.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly the gas particles push against the walls of their container.
The space a gas takes up.
A unit of temperature that starts at 0 at absolute zero.
A unit of amount for a very large number of particles, rather like a dozen for 12.
An actual gas whose particles have a size and attract one another.

gewusst: One litre of air contains about 27 thousand billion billion gas particles.
It cannot get colder than 0 kelvin, that is minus 273.15 degrees Celsius.
Of all real gases, helium behaves particularly like an ideal gas.

teile.einleitung: The Gibbs free energy, also called free enthalpy, reveals whether a chemical reaction can take place by itself. It links two quantities: the heat that is released or taken in during a reaction, and the disorder, the entropy. It is named after the American physicist Josiah Willard Gibbs.
wichtigste: The Gibbs free energy of reaction is calculated with ΔG = ΔH − T·ΔS.
At constant pressure and temperature, a reaction takes place spontaneously if ΔG is less than zero.
If ΔH is negative and ΔS positive, the reaction is spontaneous at any temperature.
Temperature can decide whether a reaction takes place spontaneously or not.
Through ΔG° = −R·T·ln K, the Gibbs free energy is linked to the equilibrium constant.
If ΔG° is exactly zero, the equilibrium constant K equals 1.
The Gibbs free energy is named after the American physicist Josiah Willard Gibbs.

abschnitte.text: **Josiah Willard Gibbs** lived from 1839 to 1903 and was a professor at Yale University in the USA. He is regarded as one of the founders of chemical **thermodynamics**, the study of energy and heat in the transformation of substances. In the 1870s he published papers on the equilibrium of substances. In them he introduced the quantity that bears his name today.

The change in Gibbs free energy is calculated with ΔG = ΔH − T·ΔS. Here ΔH is the **enthalpy of reaction**, that is the heat given off or taken in. ΔS is the change in **entropy**, which can be described in simple terms as a measure of disorder. T is the absolute temperature in kelvin. If ΔG is negative, the reaction is called **exergonic** and can take place spontaneously; if ΔG is positive, it is called endergonic.

If ΔH is negative and ΔS positive, ΔG is always negative and the reaction takes place spontaneously at any temperature. If ΔH and ΔS have the same sign, the temperature decides. When lime is burnt, CaCO₃ breaks down into CaO and CO₂, with ΔH = +178 kJ/mol and ΔS = +161 J/(mol·K). The reaction only becomes spontaneous from about 1100 kelvin, that is at about 830 degrees Celsius. An everyday example: ice only melts by itself above 0 degrees Celsius.

In the ammonia synthesis N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, ΔH° = −92.2 kJ and ΔS° = −198.7 J/K. At 298 kelvin this gives ΔG° = −92.2 kJ − 298 K · (−0.1987 kJ/K), so about −33 kJ. The reaction is therefore spontaneous at room temperature. Because ΔS is negative, ΔG becomes less favourable at higher temperatures. Ammonia is an important starting material for fertiliser.

The Gibbs free energy is linked to the **equilibrium constant** K: ΔG° = −R·T·ln K. Here R is the gas constant, 8.314 J/(mol·K). If ΔG° equals zero, K is exactly 1. With ΔG° = −5.7 kJ/mol and 298 K, K comes out at about 10. The more negative ΔG°, the more products are present at equilibrium.

A negative ΔG only says that a reaction can take place, not how fast it does so. At room temperature, diamond should actually turn into graphite, but this takes an unimaginably long time. Wood does not burn by itself either, even though combustion is exergonic; it first needs a spark. How fast a reaction is depends on the **activation energy**, not on the Gibbs free energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The heat content of a system; ΔH is the heat given off or taken in during a reaction.
A quantity that, in simple terms, describes the disorder or spreading out of energy.
A reaction with a negative ΔG that can take place spontaneously.
Unit of temperature that starts at absolute zero; 0 degrees Celsius is 273.15 kelvin.
Energy needed for a reaction to start at all.

gewusst: Our cells couple reactions with a positive ΔG to the splitting of the energy carrier ATP, which has a strongly negative ΔG.
In 1863 Gibbs received the first doctorate in engineering ever awarded in the USA, at Yale University.
Diamonds are not quite stable thermodynamically, but they still stay diamonds practically for ever.

teile.einleitung: Graphite is a soft, greyish black form of pure carbon. You use it almost every day, because the lead in a pencil is made of graphite. Although it is soft and greasy, it even conducts electricity.
wichtigste: Graphite consists of pure carbon, just like diamond.
Graphite is greyish black and feels smooth and greasy.
The lead in a pencil contains graphite and no actual lead.
The name comes from the Greek word for “to write”.
Graphite conducts electricity.
Graphite powder is good for lubricating sticking door locks.
A B on a pencil means that it writes soft and dark.

abschnitte.text: Graphite consists of many flat **layers**, in which the carbon atoms are arranged in hexagons like a honeycomb. Within a layer the atoms hold together very firmly. Between the layers, however, the forces are weak, so they slide easily over one another. That is why graphite is soft and feels greasy. Diamond also consists of carbon, but there the atoms are arranged quite differently, which is why it is extremely hard. Such different forms of the same element are called **allotropes**.

In the past, graphite was thought to be a kind of lead, which is why we still talk about pencil lead today. In reality the **lead** is made of graphite, which is mixed with clay and fired. A lot of clay makes the lead hard and light, shown by an **H**. A lot of graphite makes it soft and dark, shown by a **B**. When you write, fine flakes of graphite stay on the paper, which is why you can rub the line out. In Geneva the company Caran d'Ache has been making pencils and coloured pencils for many decades.

Electrons can move freely within the layers of graphite, so it conducts **electricity**. That is unusual for a non-metal. Graphite is therefore used for electrodes, for example in the batteries of mobile phones and electric cars. It also withstands very high temperatures without melting. That is why melting pots for metals are made from it.

Because the layers slide so easily, graphite powder is a good **lubricant**. It is sprayed, for example, into sticking door locks, where oil would attract dust. Graphite is also found in brake pads, seals and sports equipment such as tennis rackets. A single layer of graphite is called **graphene**. For research on graphene, two scientists received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2010.

Graphite occurs naturally in rocks and is mined, today mainly in China. It can also be made artificially from coal or petroleum coke. In the 16th century a particularly pure deposit of graphite was found at Borrowdale in England, and the first pencils were made with it. The mineral was given the name graphite in 1789 by the German geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner. He took it from the Greek word **graphein**, which means “to write”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A chemical element of which graphite, diamond and coal are made.
One of several forms in which the same substance can occur.
The writing stick inside a pencil.
A part through which electricity flows into or out of a substance.
A single layer of graphite only one atom thick.

gewusst: Graphite and diamond consist of exactly the same element, but they are the softest and the hardest minerals known.
With a single pencil you can draw a line several kilometres long.
There has never been real lead in pencils.

teile.einleitung: Caramel is melted and browned sugar with a sweet, slightly roasted taste. It forms when sugar is heated strongly, which changes the sugar chemically. Caramel is found in many sweets and desserts, from crème caramel to candied almonds.
wichtigste: Caramel is melted, brown sugar.
When sugar caramelises, it smells sweet and slightly roasted.
If you heat caramel for too long, it turns black and bitter.
Liquid caramel is hotter than boiling water and therefore dangerous.
Liquid caramel becomes hard as it cools.
For crème brûlée, sugar is sprinkled on the cream and browned with a flame.
Crème caramel, cream fudge and candied almonds are popular caramel treats.

abschnitte.text: Caramel forms when ordinary table sugar is heated strongly. The white sugar first melts into a clear liquid. With more heat it turns golden, then amber and finally brown. This process is called **caramelisation**.

From about 160 °C the sugar molecules start to break down and join together in new ways. Hundreds of new substances are formed, which provide **colour**, smell and flavour. At the same time water evaporates from the sugar. If it gets too hot, the sugar **chars**: it turns black, bitter and inedible.

For **crème caramel** (“Caramelköpfli” in Switzerland), liquid caramel is poured into little moulds and a custard is poured on top; when it is turned out, the sauce runs over the pudding. For crème brûlée, sugar on the cream is turned into a crunchy crust with a flame. **Cream fudge** (“Rahmtäfeli”) is cooked from sugar and cream until the mixture is light brown. Candied almonds from the fair have a coating of caramel.

Liquid caramel is much hotter than boiling water, which only reaches 100 °C. It also sticks to the skin and causes severe **burns**. Children should therefore only make caramel with adults. If you pour cold liquid into hot caramel, it can spit violently.

Strongly heated sugar is also used as a brown food colouring. This **caramel colour** colours cola, sauces and some breads dark, for example. On packaging it is listed with the number E 150. It hardly tastes sweet, because the sugar has been almost completely transformed.

What caramel is like after cooling depends on the temperature and the ingredients. Pure caramel sets glassy and hard like a boiled sweet. With cream and butter, a soft, chewy **toffee** or a sauce is made. As it cools, the mixture becomes firm because the molecules can no longer move freely.

begriffe.erklaerung: Browning sugar by heating it strongly.
A brown colouring made from strongly heated sugar, E 150.
The chemical name for ordinary table sugar.
A substance turning black because of too much heat.

gewusst: When it is being made, caramel can get hotter than 170 °C, almost twice as hot as boiling water.
Caramel contains hundreds of different flavour substances that were not in the sugar at all before.

teile.einleitung: The Haber-Bosch process is a chemical process for making ammonia from the nitrogen in the air and hydrogen. Ammonia is used above all to make artificial fertiliser. Without this process, not nearly as many people in the world could be fed today.
wichtigste: In the Haber-Bosch process, ammonia is made from nitrogen and hydrogen.
Fritz Haber discovered the reaction; the BASF engineer Carl Bosch made it usable on an industrial scale.
In 1913 the first large plant started operating in Oppau near Ludwigshafen.
The catalyst is mainly iron with promoters.
A reactor typically works at around 450 °C and very high pressure.
Today the hydrogen is usually obtained from natural gas by steam reforming.
The ammonia is separated off by cooling and liquefying it.
Gases that have not reacted are sent back into the reactor.

abschnitte.text: Plants need **nitrogen** to grow. Although the air consists of about 78 per cent nitrogen, most plants cannot use it in this form. Around 1900 people feared that natural fertiliser would no longer be enough for the growing world population. With the Haber-Bosch process, nitrogen from the air can be turned into **ammonia**. From this, artificial fertiliser is made, with which a large part of the world’s food is grown today.

Around 1909 the German chemist **Fritz Haber** showed in the laboratory that ammonia can be made from nitrogen and hydrogen. The engineer **Carl Bosch** of the company BASF turned this into a process for huge factories. In 1913 the first large plant started up in Oppau near Ludwigshafen. Haber received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the year 1918, Bosch in 1931. Haber is still controversial today, because he pushed for the use of poison gas in the First World War.

Nitrogen and hydrogen are strongly compressed, to about 150 to 300 bar. In the **reactor** they flow at around 450 °C over a **catalyst** made of iron with additives, the promoters. The reaction does give off heat, but at room temperature it would be far too slow. On each pass, only part of the gases turns into ammonia. The gas mixture is cooled so that the ammonia becomes liquid and runs off, and the remaining gases are sent back into the reactor in a **loop**.

The nitrogen is obtained from the air. Today the **hydrogen** is usually made from natural gas with a process called **steam reforming**. This produces a lot of carbon dioxide, which harms the climate. Worldwide, the Haber-Bosch process uses about one to two per cent of all energy. Researchers are working on obtaining the hydrogen from water in future, using electricity from sun and wind.

Experts estimate that without artificial fertiliser only about half as many people could be fed. Ammonia is also used to make plastics, medicines and, unfortunately, explosives too. However, too much fertiliser on the fields can pollute lakes and groundwater, for example with **nitrate**. In Switzerland, farmers therefore follow rules about how much fertiliser they may use. The process is regarded as one of the most important inventions of the 20th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sharp-smelling gas made of nitrogen and hydrogen, the basic material for fertiliser.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
The name for a reaction that gives off heat.
A process for making hydrogen from natural gas and steam.
Fertiliser made in factories, containing nutrients for plants.

gewusst: A considerable part of the nitrogen in your body has at some point passed through the Haber-Bosch process.
For the process, engineers had to develop new steel pipes that could withstand the high pressure and the hydrogen.
Ammonia is one of the chemicals produced in the largest quantities in the world.

teile.einleitung: Rubber is a stretchy material that springs back into its old shape after being pulled. Natural rubber comes from the milky sap of the rubber tree. Tyres, wellington boots, rubbers for erasing, balloons and shoe soles are made of rubber.
wichtigste: The special thing about rubber is that it is stretchy.
Natural rubber is obtained from the sap of a tree.
The milky sap of the rubber tree is called latex.
The rubber tree originally grows in the rainforest of South America.
Rubber does not let water through, which is why people like to wear wellington boots in the rain.
With a rubber you rub out pencil lines.
Balloons and the soles of trainers are usually made of rubber.

abschnitte.text: The **rubber tree** comes from the Amazon rainforest in South America. If you cut its bark at a slant, a white, milky sap flows out, called **latex**. From this the raw material **natural rubber** is obtained. Today most rubber plantations are in South East Asia, for example in Thailand and Indonesia. The workers collect the sap in small cups that hang on the trees.

Raw natural rubber is sticky when hot and hard and brittle when cold. In 1839 the American **Charles Goodyear** discovered that natural rubber becomes much better if it is heated with sulphur. This process is called **vulcanisation**. The long chains in the rubber link up with each other like a net. Only then does natural rubber become elastic, durable rubber.

Today a large part of rubber is made artificially from **crude oil**. This is called synthetic rubber. It was developed in the 20th century, when natural rubber was scarce or expensive. For many products, natural and synthetic rubber are mixed. Experts count rubber among the **elastomers**, that is plastics that can be stretched and spring back.

More than half of all rubber is used for the **tyres** of cars, lorries and bicycles. Wellington boots keep your feet dry because rubber does not let water through. Rubber soles on trainers cushion and do not slip. Seals, hoses, gloves, balls and balloons are also made of rubber. A **rubber** for erasing picks up the fine graphite particles of a pencil line and rubs them off the paper.

Old tyres can be made into rubber granules, for example for playground surfaces and artificial grass. Tyres wear down as you drive, and the fine **tyre wear particles** get into the environment as microplastics. A lot of rainforest in South East Asia has been cleared for new rubber plantations. Some people are allergic to natural latex, for example in gloves. For them there are products made of synthetic rubber.

begriffe.erklaerung: The raw material from which rubber is made.
The milky sap of the rubber tree.
Heating natural rubber with sulphur so that it becomes elastic and durable.
A material that can be stretched and springs back into its shape.

gewusst: In 1770 the English scientist Joseph Priestley noticed that you can rub out pencil lines with natural rubber.
Indigenous peoples of South America were playing with balls made of natural rubber centuries ago.
The English word “rubber” comes from “to rub”.

teile.einleitung: Green chemistry is a way of doing chemistry that produces as little waste, poison and energy use as possible. It does not only ask whether a reaction works, but also how clean and economical it is. In 1998 Paul Anastas and John Warner summed up their ideas in twelve principles.
wichtigste: Green chemistry aims to avoid waste instead of disposing of it later.
In 1998 Paul Anastas and John Warner formulated the twelve principles of green chemistry.
In 1991 Barry Trost introduced the idea of atom economy.
Addition reactions in principle have an atom economy of 100 per cent.
Roger Sheldon’s E factor shows how many kilograms of waste are produced per kilogram of product.
Catalysts are not used up and therefore save waste.
Supercritical carbon dioxide serves as an environmentally friendly solvent, for example when decaffeinating coffee.

abschnitte.text: The chemical industry makes medicines, plastics, paints and fertilisers. In the past this often produced large amounts of **waste** and poisonous by-products. Green chemistry wants to plan processes so that such problems do not arise in the first place. Important aims are fewer dangerous substances, less energy use and more **renewable raw materials**. The idea behind it is: prevention is better than clearing up.

In 1998 the US chemists **Paul Anastas** and **John Warner** published twelve principles of green chemistry. They include, for example: avoid waste, use substances that are as non-toxic as possible, and work at room temperature. Other rules call for safe solvents and for products that break down in nature after use. The principles are not laws but a kind of checklist for good chemistry. Today they are taught at many universities, including in Switzerland.

**Atom economy** was introduced by Barry Trost in 1991. It shows what percentage of the atoms from the starting substances ends up in the desired product. In the reaction of bromomethane with sodium hydroxide solution to give methanol and sodium bromide, it is only about 24 per cent; the rest becomes by-product. In **addition reactions**, in which two molecules simply join together, it is in principle 100 per cent. Roger Sheldon’s **E factor**, on the other hand, measures the amount of waste: if 50 kg of waste are produced for 2 kg of product, it is 25.

**Catalysts** speed up reactions without being used up themselves. That is why only small amounts of them are needed, which saves a lot of waste compared with substances that have to be added in large quantities. One example is **olefin metathesis**, for which Yves Chauvin, Robert Grubbs and Richard Schrock received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2005. The Nobel Committee called it a great step forward for green chemistry. Instead of poisonous solvents, water or **supercritical carbon dioxide** is often used today, which behaves like a liquid under high pressure.

When coffee is decaffeinated, supercritical carbon dioxide dissolves the caffeine out of the beans and then simply evaporates again. For the painkiller ibuprofen, an older process with six steps was replaced by a new one with only three steps, which produces much less waste. Washing powders contain enzymes that allow clothes to be washed clean even at low temperatures. Plastics made from plants and biodegradable packaging are also among the aims of green chemistry.

begriffe.erklaerung: The proportion of atoms from the starting substances that end up in the desired product.
Kilograms of waste per kilogram of product.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
A liquid in which other substances dissolve.
A substance under high pressure and high temperature that is neither really a gas nor really a liquid.

gewusst: In the production of some medicines, 25 to over 100 kilograms of waste are produced per kilogram of active ingredient.
The carbon dioxide that decaffeinates coffee can be used again and again.
In the USA there has been a special award for particularly green chemical processes since 1996.

teile.einleitung: With invisible ink you can write messages that cannot be seen on the paper. Only with a trick, such as heat or a colour, does the writing reappear. Behind it is exciting chemistry that you can try at home with lemon juice.
wichtigste: Invisible ink is a liquid whose writing is invisible once it has dried.
A simple invisible ink is lemon juice; milk works too.
It is best to write with a cotton bud.
Heat makes lemon writing visible and turns it brown.
Candle wax writing on white paper becomes visible when you paint over it with watercolour.
Writing in bicarbonate of soda water appears in colour when you brush red cabbage juice over it.
In the past, people used invisible ink for secret messages.

abschnitte.text: The best-known invisible ink is **lemon juice**. You dip a cotton bud into it and write with it on white paper. Once it has dried, almost nothing can be seen. If you warm the paper, for example with a hairdryer or an iron, the writing appears in brown. Milk, apple juice or onion juice also work in this way.

Lemon juice and milk contain sugar and other **organic substances**. When heated, these start to brown earlier than the paper, much like sugar when it caramelises. In addition, the acid in lemon juice makes the paper fibres more sensitive where you have written. So the writing turns brown while the rest of the paper stays light. Important: only heat it with the help of adults and never hold it over an open flame.

A completely different trick works with a white **candle**. You write firmly on white paper with the tip of the candle; the writing can hardly be seen. If you then paint over the sheet with watercolour, the paint runs off the wax in drops. Wax is **water-repellent**, so the writing stays white while the paper around it takes on colour.

Red cabbage juice contains dyes that change colour depending on whether a substance is acidic or alkaline. Such a substance is called an **indicator**. If you write with bicarbonate of soda water, which is alkaline, and then brush red cabbage juice over it, the writing appears greenish or blue. If you write with lemon juice or vinegar instead, the writing turns pink to red. This way you can even send coloured secret messages.

As early as ancient times, scholars described how you can write invisibly with plant juices. Over the centuries, merchants, diplomats and spies used invisible inks to hide messages. Especially in the two World Wars, secret messages were written between the harmless lines of a letter. Hiding messages is called **steganography**. Today digital encryption is usually used instead.

There are pens with ink that only glows under **UV light**; often a small lamp is built right in. Similar substances protect banknotes against forgery: on Swiss franc notes, certain patterns light up under UV light. Entry stamps at concerts or festivals are also often only visible under UV light.

begriffe.erklaerung: Ink that is invisible after drying and only becomes visible through a trick.
A substance that changes colour depending on whether something is acidic or alkaline.
A surface on which water forms drops and runs off instead of soaking in.
The art of hiding messages so that nobody notices they exist.
Light that is invisible to humans and makes some substances glow.

gewusst: With red cabbage juice you can create different colours in a single message, depending on whether you wrote with something acidic or alkaline.
Sweat from your fingers also leaves invisible traces, which the police can make visible with special powders.
Many banknotes contain fibres that only glow in colour under UV light.

teile.einleitung: A mixture forms when you put two or more substances together without a new substance being created. Muesli, sand with stones or salad dressing are mixtures. The exciting part is that mixtures can be separated back into their parts.
wichtigste: A mixture consists of at least two substances that do not combine chemically.
In some mixtures you can see the individual parts, for example in muesli.
In other mixtures you cannot see the parts, for example in salt water.
Oil and water do not mix; after a while the oil floats on top.
With a sieve you separate large parts from small ones.
With a magnet you can get iron out of a mixture.

abschnitte.text: If you pour sand and stones together, you get a **mixture**. Each substance keeps its properties: the stones stay hard and the sand stays grainy. Muesli is also a mixture of flakes, nuts and fruit. In contrast, a chemical reaction creates a completely **new substance**.

In a **heterogeneous mixture** you can recognise the different parts with the naked eye or with a magnifying glass. Examples are muesli, granite or sand with stones. In a **homogeneous mixture** everything looks the same, even though several substances are in it. Salt water, air and squash are such mixtures.

You can shake oil and water hard, but after a short time they separate again. The oil is lighter and floats on top. With the help of egg or mustard, however, you can combine the two into an **emulsion**; this is how mayonnaise is made, for example. Milk is also an emulsion of tiny droplets of fat in water.

You separate pasta from the cooking water with a **sieve**, and peas and rice can also be separated this way. You get iron nails out of sand with a **magnet**. You can pour dirty water through a coffee filter; this is called **filtering**. If you let salt water evaporate, the salt is left behind.

If you mix blue and yellow paint, it turns green, and yet both dyes are still in it. Concrete is a mixture of cement, sand, gravel and water. In Switzerland, salt is obtained from salty water in **salt works** such as those at Schweizerhalle or Bex. In sewage treatment plants, dirt is separated from waste water so that clean water can flow back into rivers and lakes.

begriffe.erklaerung: Several substances together that have not combined into a new substance.
A mixture of two liquids that do not normally mix, such as oil and water.
Pouring a mixture through a fine filter so that solid parts are caught.
When water slowly turns into water vapour and disappears.

gewusst: The air we breathe is also a mixture of several gases.
Gold panners separate gold from sand because gold is much heavier and stays behind in the pan.
In Swiss streams such as the Grosse Fontanne in the Napf area, hobby gold prospectors also pan gold out of the sand.

teile.einleitung: Calorimetry is the measurement of amounts of heat that are released or used up in chemical reactions, in melting or in burning. The measuring device is called a calorimeter. It is used, for example, to find out how much energy there is in food or fuels.
wichtigste: Calorimetry is the measurement of amounts of heat.
Liquid water has a specific heat capacity of about 4.18 J/(g·K).
200 g of water take in about 4.2 kJ of heat when warmed by 5 K.
The calorimeter constant shows how much heat the device itself takes in per kelvin.
A Dewar flask prevents heat losses.
A bomb calorimeter measures the change in internal energy at constant volume.
Unlike the net calorific value, the gross calorific value includes the heat of condensation of water.
Lavoisier and Laplace built an ice calorimeter in the 1780s.

abschnitte.text: The word **calorimetry** comes from the Latin calor for “heat” and the Greek metron for “measure”. In many reactions heat is released; they are called **exothermic**. In others heat is taken in; they are called endothermic. A **calorimeter** measures how large these amounts of heat are. Usually this is done by measuring how much a known amount of water warms up. Heat is given in joules or kilojoules.

To warm 1 gram of water by 1 kelvin, you need about 4.18 joules. This value is called the **specific heat capacity**. The heat is calculated as mass times heat capacity times temperature change. If 200 g of water warm up by 5 K, they have therefore taken in about 4.2 kJ. Because the container and the thermometer also absorb some heat, the **calorimeter constant** of the device is determined first.

If you mix 50 mL of hydrochloric acid and 50 mL of sodium hydroxide solution, each at 1 mol/L, the solution warms up by about 6.8 K. The 100 g of solution have taken in about 2.8 kJ of heat. Because 0.05 mol of acid were neutralised, this gives an **enthalpy of neutralisation** of about minus 57 kJ per mole. The minus sign shows that the reaction gives off heat. For such experiments a double-walled, evacuated **Dewar flask** is often used, similar to a vacuum flask.

In a **bomb calorimeter**, a sample burns in a tightly sealed steel container with pure oxygen. The container stands in a water bath, whose warming is measured precisely. Because the volume stays the same, the change in **internal energy** is measured directly. This is how the energy content of food, wood, heating oil or coal is determined. The **gross calorific value** also includes the heat released when the water vapour formed turns liquid again; the net calorific value does not.

In the 1780s the French scientists Antoine Lavoisier and Pierre-Simon Laplace built an **ice calorimeter**. They measured heat by how much ice melted, and even used it to study the heat given off by a live guinea pig. Heat used to be given in **calories**; 1 kilocalorie corresponds to about 4.18 kilojoules. On food packaging in Switzerland, both figures, kJ and kcal, are still given today. Modern condensing boilers use the heat of condensation of the water vapour and so save energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device for measuring amounts of heat.
The heat that 1 gram of a substance needs to warm up by 1 kelvin.
The name for a reaction that gives off heat.
A double-walled container with a vacuum in between, like a vacuum flask.
All the heat released when a substance burns, including the heat of condensation.

gewusst: Lavoisier and Laplace used a live guinea pig for their measurements.
The vacuum flask goes back to the Dewar flask, which James Dewar invented in 1892.
Water can store a particularly large amount of heat, which is why lakes and seas even out the climate.
